News.title: ‘I thought my breast milk was coming in - it was actually a sign of stage 3 cancer’
News.content:
‘I thought my breast milk was coming in - it was actually a sign of stage 3 cancer’

Mum-of-two Alex now worries if she'll be able to see her children grown up

View 4 Images A pregnant mum thought her hard breast tissue was her milk coming in early - but it turned out to be breast cancer (Image: Alex Cheshire-Round© SWNS)

A pregnant mum was “shocked” to discover that she had cancer, after thinking a symptom was actually just her breast milk coming in. Alex Cheshire-Round assumed her hardened breast tissue at 24 weeks was a sign her milk was arriving early.

‌



The 29-year-old was expecting her second child when she noticed firmness on her right breast while rolling over in bed in May. She had begun leaking milk at 18 weeks pregnant with her firstborn, Ronnie, now 10 months old, so believed it was occurring again.

‌



However, her husband, Tom Cheshire-Round, 31, encouraged her to get it examined and a biopsy and scans confirmed she had stage three breast cancer. Alex had a half-centimetre lump removed from her breast and lymph nodes extracted from under her right arm at Coventry hospital.

‌



Five minutes after she woke from the operation, her baby was distressed, and Alex was put under again and her daughter, Lexi, was born at 1.57pm weighing 4lb 13oz at 33 weeks.

Alex is now awaiting confirmation of what further treatment she will require, but believes chemotherapy is probable.

View 4 Images Alex Cheshire-Round, 29, was 24 weeks pregnant with her second child when she noticed hardness on her right breast. Picture: Alex Cheshire-Round© SWNS (Image: Alex Cheshire-Round© SWNS)

‌



Alex, from Nuneaton in Warwickshire, who works in sales, said: "This is very scary and was a huge shock. I just shrugged it off at first - you go through so many changes when you're pregnant.

"It's so rare for someone my age to get breast cancer. I just thought it must be something to do with pregnancy and hormonal changes. My milk came in early in my pregnancy with Ronnie, I reassured myself it was just that happening again.

"I got really worried when my GP said they don't give mammograms for under 40s, but then offered me one after inspecting it. We're lucky we decided to have our children close in age, because the treatment might affect my fertility.

‌



View 4 Images Her husband Tom urged her to have it checked out and a biopsy and scans revealed she had stage three breast cancer. Picture: Alex Cheshire-Round© SWNS (Image: Alex Cheshire-Round© SWNS)

"Women feel insecure enough about our looks after having a baby, this is much worse for me now as I'm also worrying about hair loss and being tired from chemotherapy." Alex and Tom, an engineer, discovered they were expecting their second child in December 2025. Lexi and Ronnie are “Irish twins” - children born less than 12 months apart.

Alex first noticed something was different with her breast as she rolled over in bed in the early hours of May 21, and visited her GP on May 26.

‌



She underwent a mammogram at George Eliot Hospital during the first week of June, where medics spotted swollen lymph nodes and carried out a biopsy. A week later, she received the devastating news that she had at least stage two cancer and required further tests.

Following MRI and CT scans, Alex was told her cancer was stage three on July 9. The scans revealed the cancer had not spread to her heart, liver or lungs, though a full-body CT scan was not possible due to her pregnancy.

View 4 Images Now Alex "worries" about whether she'll be able to see her children grow up. Picture: Alex Cheshire-Round© SWNS (Image: Alex Cheshire-Round© SWNS)

‌



Just two days before her operation, Alex was diagnosed with gestational diabetes, requiring close monitoring of her blood sugar levels. Baby Lexi was taken to the special care unit following her birth, where she was placed on oxygen and given a feeding tube.

Alex was discharged from hospital on July 18, while Lexi was transferred to George Eliot Hospital on July 20, which is nearer to home making it more convenient for Alex to visit.

Alex underwent genetic testing due to having received 30 months of chemotherapy as a child, following her diagnosis with lymphoblastic lymphoma at the age of four. She said: "This feels very unlucky! I worry about whether I'll be able to see my children grow up.

‌



Longevity expert's five health tips for people in their 30s to do now READ MORE :

"A lot of women are planners - it's really hard when you don't know if you can plan for your future. Other days I just enjoy each moment and look forward to the next.

"I'm so excited to have my little girl, but I worry about it being hard to bond with both my children while I'm going through chemo." Alex, who shared her story on Talk to the Press, urged others to seek help if they notice anything “unusual”.

She said: "Anything unusual with your body get it checked out straight away, check and double check. If you're pregnant, don't assume any changes are to do with that or your hormones, get it checked out.

‌



"Also, if you have a cancer diagnosis, you don't have to deal with this on your own, it's so much easier when you talk about it."

Breast cancer symptoms

According to the NHS, symptoms of breast cancer in women may include:

‌



A lump, or swelling in your breast, chest or armpit

A change in the skin of your breast, such as dimpling (may look like orange peel) or redness (may be harder to see on black or brown skin)

A change in size or shape of one or both breasts

Nipple discharge (if you are not pregnant or breastfeeding), which may have blood in it

A change in the shape or look of your nipple, such as it turning inwards (inverted nipple) or a rash on it (may look like eczema)

The NHS said: “You may get pain in your breast or armpit with these symptoms. But you can have these symptoms without any pain.”

It’s also important to note that men can get breast cancer, although it is rare. You should see a GP if:

Article continues below

You have a lump or swelling in your breast, chest or armpit

You have any changes in your breasts or nipples that are not normal for you

You have pain in your breast or armpit, and there are other people in your family who've had breast cancer or ovarian cancer

The NHS added: “It's important to check your breasts regularly so you know what's normal for you. This makes it easier to notice any changes in the size, look or feel of your breasts.”

News.title: Argentina forced to make change as FIFA ruling emerges after World Cup final
News.content:
Argentina forced to make change as FIFA ruling emerges after World Cup final

Argentina's disgraced team will be forced to make a change following their World Cup final loss

View 3 Images Argentina must make an alteration following the World Cup (Image: Getty)

Argentina are set to be given another brutal reminder of their devastating World Cup final defeat. The thuggish and negative tactics employed by Lionel Scaloni's side proved in vain as Spain clinched a deserved victory thanks to Ferran Torres's extra-time strike.

‌



Argentina had been aiming to lift the trophy for the fourth time in their history after Lionel Messi inspired the team to glory at Qatar 2022. Since becoming world champions, their strip had featured a gold crest displaying an outline of the trophy alongside the words "FIFA World Champions 2022".

‌



However, that prized addition to their iconic colour scheme must now be removed, as they are no longer world champions. Spain will now don the coveted emblem at the next World Cup, which they will co-host with Portugal and Morocco, with special one-off opening matches taking place in Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay to mark the 100th anniversary of the World Cup.

‌



Argentina can at least continue to display a badge commemorating their Copa America victory in 2024, a title they will defend in 2028.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Argentina failed to relinquish the World Cup trophy or the gold badge with any grace. Leandro Paredes, along with team-mate Nahuel Molina and Argentina coach Roberto Ayala, were involved in the brawl seconds after the final whistle at the MetLife Stadium.

‌



Argentina president goes on rant as calls for country to be banned from World Cup grow READ MORE :

Argentina FA intervene as World Cup final conspiracy theories emerge after Spain win READ MORE :

Contrary to the belief at the time, Paredes was not shown a red card following the incident. But FIFA has announced that its disciplinary committee has appointed a disciplinary and ethics prosecutor to investigate possible breaches of the FIFA disciplinary code.

The South Americans attracted further condemnation for their combative style, with Chelsea's Enzo Fernandez sent off for two yellow cards.

View 3 Images Argentina must give up the gold badge in the centre of their shirt (Image: Getty Images)

‌



A FIFA statement read: "Following an assessment of the relevant match reports for the FIFA World Cup final between Spain and Argentina, and in line with article 36 of the FIFA disciplinary code (FDC), the FIFA disciplinary committee has appointed a disciplinary and ethics prosecutor to investigate potential breaches of the FDC with regard to the post-match incidents."

Retrospective punishments, such as fines and/or suspensions, are possible for the country's federation or individuals. However, Spain midfielder Gavi, who was grabbed by Paredes during the post-match melee, insists he doesn't not want the Boca Juniors star to be hit with a ban.

View 3 Images Leandro Paredes drags Gavi to the floor (Image: Marvin Ibo Guengoer - GES Sportfoto, Getty Images)

‌



Gavi told El Partidazo de COPE: "I don't think [Paredes] should be suspended. I understand it's not a good image for children, but I think there's also that side to football, which is a bit more physical, more aggressive.

"The most logical thing would have been to send him off during the match, and that's it. In the end, I think it's all football, and it has to be that way."

News.title: How suspicious public fell in love with horse-drawn monster that became nation's favourite gadget
News.content:
Next time you whizz your vacuum cleaner over your carpets, spare a thought for Puffing Billy. For it’s been 125 years since esteemed British engineer Hubert Cecil Booth invented the first motorised carpet cleaner… and it was a monster. The 1901 version of today’s upright, cylinder, bagless or even robot vac was a petrol-driven, horse-drawn machine, which used suction to pull dirt through a cloth filter.

Because of its massive size, workers parked it on the street and fed hoses through people’s windows. Legend has it that Booth realised suction was the key to true cleaning, after placing a handkerchief over a restaurant chair, sucking air through it, and seeing the massive amount of dust trapped.

Household historian Laura Humphreys says: “The original machines were far too large to use indoors. Booth founded the British Vacuum Cleaner and Engineering Company, offering a mobile cleaning service where his bright red, horse-drawn vacuums would park on the street and snake long hoses up to 100 feet into clients' windows.”

View 7 Images The British Vacuum Cleaner Company, was founded in 1900 by Henry Cecil Booth (1871-1955) (Image: SSPL via Getty Images)

‌



Soon carpet cleaning became a posh party piece. Laura continues: “The novelty was an instant hit among London high society, leading to ‘vacuum parties’ where society ladies would invite friends over to watch the rugs being cleaned. Booth even used his invention to clean the carpets at Buckingham Palace for King Edward VII and Queen Victoria's households.”

Puffing Billy was inspired by a manual carpet sweeper, patented in 1811 by British inventor James Hume, and combining a rotating brush and bellows to generate suction - but Booth’s motorised version was the great great grandparent to the 6.4 million vacuum cleaners sold annually in the UK today.

Ironically, when more user friendly models came into play, there was a certain stigma attached to using them. Laura, who is curatorial lead (Collections & Digital) at the Science Museum Group, says they were considered to be lazy, as rugs no longer had to be taken outside and beaten. They could be cleaned where they were. She explains: ”Hard work was believed to be good for you. And the invention of the vacuum cleaner made housework less hard.

View 7 Images The 1930s introduced lightweight plastics like Bakelite to replace heavy metal bodies. (Image: Archive Photos)

‌



“Books and periodicals said, ‘you should still be using a carpet beater.’ ‘You should still be using the old ways’. There was also a moral objection to them, as the thought was, ‘Physical labour is good for you’. ‘It's good for your servants to work hard’. ‘Don't make life too easy for them’.”

In 1908, Ohio janitor James Spangler invented the first portable electric vacuum. It used an electric fan motor, a broomstick and a pillowcase. Heralding the modern era of carpet cleaning, he sold the patent to William Henry Hoover in 1908 and his company became so synonymous with this form of cleaning that "hoovering" became a universal term.

But the machines were initially super expensive. Laura says: “They were huge industrial machines in the early 20th century. They start to come down to domestic scale around about the 1920s and you had brands like Hoover and Electrolux.”

View 7 Images Hoover cConstellation vacuum cleaner & attachments circa 1956 (Image: Science Museum Group Collection)

‌



Rich families bought early models to tempt servants to work for them. Laura says: “Everybody tends to think of the Downton Abbey, Gosford Park army of servants in the stately home. But the vast majority of servants - mainly women - were actually working alone as a sole employee in a middle-class house.

“In the 1920s, more employment opportunities began to open up for women. Therefore, cleaners became harder to get. Families needed to find new ways to do their domestic work and also attract servants. This is where a vacuum came in. You’d get adverts for servants mentioning the kind of technology they have in their home to help them.”

The 1930s saw the invention of one of the UK’s biggest vacuum cleaners at Eltham Palace. Featuring an advanced, built-in, centralised vacuum cleaning system and installed by wealthy owners Stephen and Virginia Courtauld, the system used a large suction pump in the basement, connected to hidden wall outlets throughout the Art Deco mansion. Laura’s favourite cleaner, she says: “That was cutting edge and very much of the time that the palace was built.”

View 7 Images Artwork by John Hassall. This poster shows a maid running in alarm from a vacuum cleaner which extends in through the window (Image: SSPL via Getty Images)

‌



The 1930s also introduced lightweight plastics like Bakelite to replace heavy metal bodies, streamlining shapes and lowering total weight. And the decade saw the invention of disposable bags by the firm Air-Way. Widely adopted in the 1950s, the multi-layer cellulose fibre bags eliminated the messy chore of shaking out reusable cloth sacks.

In 1954, vacuuming took another hi-tech turn with the Hoover Constellation. Designed by Henry Dreyfuss, this spherical canister used its own exhaust air to float across the floor like a hovercraft. Then in 1969, the Hoover Company introduced power-driven wheels that moved the heavy upright machine forwards and backwards with minimal effort.

The 1960s also popularised flexible canister designs, with long hoses and swivelling nozzles, making it easier to clean bare floors, stairs, and drapes. Then, in 1978, James Dyson came along. Dismantling his failing vacuum cleaner, he found a major flaw - dust was clogging the bag and killing the suction.

View 7 Images James Dyson and his original Dyson (Image: Science Museum)

‌



Inspired by an industrial cyclone tower he’d built to separate paint particles from the air, he adapted centrifugal technology for the home and, 5,127 prototypes later, he created the world's first bagless vacuum. James says: “When I saw industrial cyclones sucking up sawdust, my instincts kicked in.”

Dyson’s first cleaner went on sale in 1986 in Japan as the G-Force, while the first model sold as a Dyson launched in May 1993 in the UK. Within 18 months it became the biggest seller in the UK. James says: “Fifteen years of invention, frustration and determination was beginning to pay off. “

At £200, it was three times the price of other vacuum cleaners, but he says: “Those choosing it recognised its technological advantage over existing designs.” And customers loved the fact they could see the dirt being sucked up, because of its transparent container. James adds: “They were fascinated by the sight of just how much dirt they had successfully cleaned up.”

View 7 Images Booth's original Red Trolley British Vacuum Cleaner, 1905 (Image: Science Museum Group Collection)

‌



And now, in 2026, 125 years since its invention, vacuum cleaner technology features hot-water active mopping, AI-driven dirt/stain detection, and self-washing roller systems. Catrin Davies, Senior SDA Product Manager at Hoover and Haier UK & Ireland, says: “The archive photos show how tastes have changed – from the retro 1950s styles to the bold 1980s designs, and now chic examples in pastel colours. Modern consumers are making fashion-forward choices when they choose their vacuum cleaners.”

Yet, while new household gadgets have many of us hooked, historian Laura says there is one tool that is still likely to give the latest vacuum cleaners a good beating. She says: Modern vacuums take just as much labour as the very first ones. Labour-saving technology is a marketing term. Want to truly save time? Buy yourself a carpet beater.”

News.title: Southport killer Axel Rudakabuna 'manipulated the system' to obtain transfer to secure hospital
News.content:
Southport killer Axel Rudakabuna 'manipulated the system' to obtain transfer to secure hospital

Axel Rudakubana 'played the system' to get a move from HMP Belmarsh to the high-security psychiatric hospital Broadmoor, the Prison Officers' Association said

View 4 Images Axel Rudakubana has been moved to Broadmoor Hospital (Image: PA)

Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has "played the system" to get a move to Broadmoor Hospital, the Prison Officers' Association said.

‌



Rudakubana murdered Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, Bebe King, six, and Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, and injured eight other children and two adults in an attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in Southport in July 2024.

‌



On Thursday, the Ministry of Justice (MoJ) confirmed the killer was transferred from HMP Belmarsh to Broadmoor, the high-security psychiatric hospital in Berkshire. A spokesperson said he would remain locked up and is unlikely to ever be released.

‌



Chris Walker, of Bond Turner, who is representing the three bereaved families, said that while this news "would devastate them at any time, the fact that this has occurred as we approach the second anniversary in our view is another move by AR who would appear to be attempting, once again, to manipulate the system".

View 4 Images (left to right) Southport victims Bebe King, six, Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, and Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine (Image: Merseyside Police/PA Wire)

He added: "We have been given the barest of details and whilst we are supporting the families through this we are urgently seeking a meeting with the appropriate authorities to understand the situation before commenting further."

‌



Chairman of the Prison Officers' Association Mark Fairhurst said Rudakubana, now 19, "played the system" and will now enjoy certain freedoms at Broadmoor, where he will be classed as a patient.

"This vile offender has played the system and will now enjoy the freedoms that are afforded mentally unwell patients in secure psychiatric hospitals, including benefits that law abiding tax payers will fund," Fairhurst said.

"My members will be placed at risk without the protections afforded to staff in prisons because he is now classed as a patient. He should spend his entire sentence in a prison in solitary confinement.

‌



View 4 Images Axel Rudakubana has been moved to Broadmoor hospital in Berkshire (Image: PA)

"My thoughts are with the families of the victims and all those affected by his heinous crimes."

Junior housing minister and former prison officer Sally Jameson said it would not be right for Rudakubana to qualify for benefits at Broadmoor.

‌



"It's not right, and I sincerely hope that he won't be qualifying for benefits. But actually, fundamentally, what I think is important to note is he will not get time off his sentence, and he will be returned to jail as soon as possible," Jameson told LBC.

The MP said high security hospitals are not like ordinary hospitals, and that Rudakubana "will be kept under very stringent conditions, befitting actually to his crime, but also the level of security that needs to be put around him".

"I'm confident that he will be returned to prison as soon as possible and serve out his sentence," she added. "And I agree that should be under the most punitive and solitary conditions that is possible."

‌



View 4 Images Floral tributes at the scene of the attack in Southport (Image: AP)

Rudakubana, from Banks, Lancashire, was jailed for life in January 2025, with a minimum sentence of 52 years for the murders of Elsie Dot Stancombe, Bebe King, and Alice da Silva Aguiar.

He also pleaded guilty to the attempted murders of Leanne Lucas and Jonathan Hayes and admitted the possession of a bladed article in a public place, namely a kitchen knife with a curved blade.

‌



His move to Broadmoor was approved by officials on behalf of ministers, but the Ministry of Justice stressed it does not alter his 52-year sentence.

A spokesperson said: "The families of those murdered and injured in Southport will be in this country's heart forever and our thoughts remain with them.

"Any decision to transfer an offender is made following an independent, clinical assessment, under the Mental Health Act.

Article continues below

"Following rigorous security checks, the offender has been transferred to a high-security psychiatric unit, where he will remain until assessed fit to return to prison.

"Officials have approved this transfer, on behalf of Ministers. This transfer does not change his sentence – which remains at 52 years – and of which he will serve every single day."

News.title: Lifebuoys were 'not recommended' on Mersea beach where mum and daughter died
News.content:
Lifebuoys were 'not recommended' on Mersea beach where mum and daughter died

A risk assessment of public rescue equipment on the West Mersea beach where Shally Rahman, 41, and Samiha, 15, died was carried out just four months ago, Colchester Council confirmed

Girl and woman in 40s die at Mersea Island beach

Colchester Council has confirmed an independent beach risk assessment 'did not recommend the installation of public rescue equipment' on the Mersea beach where a mother and daughter died this week.

‌



The risk assessment took place just four months before this week's tragedy. According to the local council the assessment concluded that, due to factors including the beach profile, tidal range and lateral currents, "public rescue equipment would be unlikely to be deployed effectively in an emergency and was therefore not recommended."

‌



Essex Police has confirmed a mum and her daughter - named as Shally Rahman, 41, and Samiha, 15, died - after getting into difficulty in water on Mersea Island at around 5.35pm on Wednesday 22 July.

‌



View 4 Images Shally Rahman died in the incident off West Mersea Beach

Dramatic footage shows the 'miracle' rescue of two boys who were seconds from death READ MORE :

Shally and Samiha had tried in vain to save Samiha's seven-year-old cousin from the water in an area of beach near Seaview Avenue at West Mersea Island Beach in Essex. The mother and daughter were reportedly caught in the high tide and, despite the the valiant efforts of teenagers on the beach, were pronounced dead at the scene. The little boy is fighting for his life in hospital.

‌



Witness describes distressing scenes

Beach hut owner Beverly Smit, 60, of West Mersea in Essex, said she heard the emergency response and went to see what was going on.

Ms Smit, who works for a local dentist, said: "By that time they were re-sussing the person on the beach, the helicopters were still in the fields."

She said that she spoke to a day tripper who had rented a neighbouring beach hut and had tried to help. She said: "He saw and they were calling for help and the children and adults were out there. He swam out I think three times.

‌



"Two of the children he brought back were not in good condition. It's not an easy swim when the tide's coming in, you're swimming against the tide, the water yesterday was particularly quite cold."

The beach hut owner added that she and members of her rowing club have helped save people in the sea previously. Ms Smit described the incident as a "massive scale of rescue and tragedy really".

View 4 Images Lifeboat at the scene in West Mersea (Image: BBC)

‌



Detective Chief Inspector Al Pitcher said: “My thoughts, and those of my team, are with the friends and family of the woman and girl who died yesterday. We can now confirm they were a mother and daughter from London and we are supporting their family in what is an unimaginable time.

“Since yesterday we have been working to establish the circumstances which led up to this incident. At this stage we believe they were trying to help a seven year-old boy who had got into difficulties.

“The boy was taken to hospital where he remains in a critical condition but the woman and teenage girl, sadly, died. All the people involved in this incident are related to each other.

‌



“As part of our investigation we are working through speaking to dozens of witnesses and taking their accounts, and we are building a picture of what happened. These enquiries are ongoing and I need anyone who has any information to get in contact.

“Finally, I want to thank the first responders who worked tirelessly to try save their lives and I want to pay tribute to their efforts.”

View 4 Images Prime Minister Andy Burnham has vowed to support local authorities following the deaths. (Image: Getty)

‌



Andy Burnham says tragedies highlight the dangers of swimming in open water

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has vowed to support local authorities following the deaths. Mr Burnham said he was "so sad to hear the news" but admitted he did not have the details of the case.

He added: "It does bring over, sometimes, the dangers of open water swimming at this time of the year. I just would ask people to consider that. But thank you to the emergency services who stepped in and of course, you know, we will work to support the local authorities as we get to the bottom of this."

Colchester Council statemen

View 4 Images A teenage girl and a woman in her 40s have died after a group got into difficulty in the water at the beach of a holiday park (Image: PA)

‌



A Colchester Council spokesperson said: “We are aware of views that have been expressed regarding additional public rescue equipment. However, decisions on water safety measures are informed by professional risk assessments and advice from specialist organisations.

“As part of our risk assessment process for the site, the council commissioned an independent RLSS UK beach risk assessment in March 2026, which did not recommend the installation of public rescue equipment within the assessed area of West Mersea beach.

“The assessment concluded that, due to factors including the beach profile, tidal range and lateral currents, public rescue equipment would be unlikely to be deployed effectively in an emergency and was therefore not recommended on that stretch of coastline.

‌



“We continue to work closely with partner organisations through the Mersea Water Safety Forum, a multi-agency partnership that brings together organisations with expertise and responsibilities in water safety.

“Together, the forum assesses local risks and develops and implements measures to help improve safety in and around the water.”

Cllr David King, Deputy Leader and Portfolio Holder for Local Government Reorganisation, Communities and Public Protection, added: "Everyone at Colchester City Council is deeply saddened by the tragic loss of two people following the incident at West Mersea.

‌



"Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with their families, friends and all those affected by this devastating incident. We would also like to pay tribute to the emergency services and volunteers who responded.

"This tragedy is a stark reminder of the importance of taking care in and around the water. We encourage everyone visiting any coastline this summer to follow water safety advice and take appropriate precautions to help keep themselves and others safe."

The Mirror has launched the Save Lives For Sam water safety campaign to tackle the UK's growing drowning crisis. Backed by MPs, Olympic champions, national water safety organisations and bereaved families, the campaign is calling for urgent action to make our waters safer.

News.title: Yellow heat alert warnings issued for 6 counties as temperatures to hit 30C - full list
News.content:
Yellow heat alert warnings issued for 6 counties as temperatures to hit 30C - full list

Heat health warnings are in place for part of the UK as the country faces further high temperatures which could reach 30C with a "risk to life" for vulnerable people

View 2 Images The UK faces further high temperatures in the coming days (Image: Amer Ghazzal/Shutterstock)

Brits face more scorching temperatures with highs of 30C with heat health warnings in place.

‌



Many parts of England are in prolonged dry weather status as the country has received just 3% of its average July rainfall, with hosepipe bans in place for 23 million customers and suppliers warning they may stay in place all summer.

‌



Wildfires have been raging in a number of places in England, while Scotland has also been hit by a major wildfire in the Cairngorms, and in the Republic of Ireland, a nationwide hosepipe ban is in place in response to the dry conditions.

‌



And yellow heat health alerts issued for the East Midlands, East of England, London, South East, South West and West Midlands are in place from 9am on Friday until 9am on Sunday.

View 2 Images A map showing parts of the country with heat health alerts (Image: UK Health Security Agent)

Temperatures in the affected areas are forecast to reach mid to high 20s, with a high of 30C a possibility, as much of the country continues to experience a prolonged period of dry, warm weather.

‌



The heat health warning from the UK Health Security Agency comes as drought was declared in North Wales and the Upper Severn, following record dry conditions, heatwaves, wildfires and dwindling rivers.

It is the first part of the UK to declare drought status amid a summer of record-breaking heatwaves.

This summer’s dry conditions follow last year’s drought summer, as the UK increasingly faces more extreme weather fuelled by human-caused climate change, mostly from burning fossil fuels.

‌



Risk in heat alert areas

Minor impacts are expected across health and social care services, including:

increased use of healthcare services by vulnerable people

greater risk to life of vulnerable people

increased potential for indoor environments to become very warm

water‑related incidents may increase, including risks from cold‑water shock and drowning

The Met Office said temperatures could reach 30C in parts of South East England on Friday while parts of Scotland and Northern Ireland will see patches of cloud.

‌



Forecaster Craig Snell said outbreaks of rain will move southwards on Saturday, spreading from Scotland and Northern Ireland into northern England and parts of Wales. By Sunday, temperatures are expected to turn “fresher” across much of the UK, with rain possible in “areas that haven’t seen much” over the past few weeks, he added.

The heat alerts are in place at the beginning of a stretch in which millions of motorists are expected to take to the roads for summer getaways.

The AA said around 6.3 million drivers are planning a road trip of more than 100 miles between Friday and Thursday. The Port of Dover is expecting another busy weekend but has worked to smooth any delays caused by new EU border checks.

News.title: Major search for two men last seen going to the sea near Haven holiday park in North Wales
News.content:
Major search for two men last seen going to the sea near Haven holiday park in North Wales

Two men are missing after they were last seen with inflatable kayaks at a beach near Hafan-y-Mor, Pwllheli, North Wales - a major search effort is underway

View 3 Images Hafan Y Mor holiday park on the North Wales coast (file image)

A desperate search is underway for two missing men last seen with inflatable kayaks at a beach in Wales.

‌



The pair, named only as Simon and Connor, were close to a Haven Holiday Park on Tuesday evening and were believed to be heading towards the coast near Hafan-y-Mor, Pwllheli, North Wales.

‌



Coastguards and the RNLI have launched a major search effort, with witnesses urged to contact police if they have any information about the pair's whereabouts.

‌



View 3 Images Connor (Image: North Wales Police)

A spokesperson for North Wales Police said: "Concerns were raised for the whereabouts of Simon and Connor, who were last seen in the vicinity of the beach off Hafan-Y-Mor, Pwllheli at approximately 6.30pm on Tuesday 21st July.

‌



"They were believed to be heading to the beach with inflatable kayaks."

Chief Inspector Ian Roberts said: "Officers are conducting enquiries and searching in the locality, supported by colleagues from HM Coastguard.

View 3 Images Simon (Image: North Wales Police)

Article continues below

"If you were on the beach on Tuesday evening, or have any information that could help us find Simon and Connor, please contact us via our live webchat or on 101 quoting reference O118860."

News.title: 'My best friend ruined my wedding day'
News.content:
Dear Coleen,

I got married in May and my best friend, who I’ve known since I was 13, behaved really badly in the run-up to the wedding and on the day itself.

I was focused on the arrangements and enjoying my wedding day, but now I’ve had time to process it, I’m getting more and more annoyed with her attitude and don’t know how I should talk to her about it.

First of all, instead of being happy for me, she was either negative or disinterested, then when it came to the hen do, she made me change the date to fit in with her schedule and later said she couldn’t make it at the last minute. She couldn’t care less that everyone else put themselves out for her.

On the wedding day itself, she showed up in an off-white maxi dress, which raised a few eyebrows, but I let it slide and told her she looked great. She went back to her hotel early, so missed the cake-cutting and dancing and, in every single photo taken from the day, she has a face like a wet weekend.

‌



View 3 Images The reader says: "She's really let me down." (Image: Getty Images)

I feel she’s really let me down and hasn’t behaved like a friend. I understand she’s had a rough time with relationships and has been single forever, but I feel hurt if she’s taking it out on me. What do I do?

Coleen says,

Ouch! I think weddings can bring out the worst in some people unfortunately. But the main thing is not to let whatever is going on spoil your memories of your special day.

It sounds like you navigated it well and had a fantastic time with your other friends and your family, so that’s what matters. As for your friend, I think this attention-seeking behaviour could be down to jealousy, but it’s probably less about you and more to do with her own unhappiness or insecurities.

‌



Your wedding perhaps brought it home to her that she’s not where she wants to be in her life, but of course that’s no excuse to behave badly and try to spoil things for you. Don’t let her think she’s got under your skin.

View 3 Images Coleen says: "People change, life takes you on different paths, circumstances intervene and so on." (Image: Getty Images/iStockphoto)

If I were you, I’d say something like, “I had such an amazing time at the wedding and everyone else loved it, but you didn’t seem to enjoy yourself. Is there anything going on?”

Maybe you’ll get some honesty from her that’ll help you move on positively as friends but if you don’t, then let it go and focus on enjoying this exciting time in your life.

‌



It’s hard when something shifts in a close, long-standing friendship, but it happens and people change, life takes you on different paths, circumstances intervene and so on. You might always know each other, but just not in the way you did when you were younger.

Coleen’s words of wisdom

I’m not a fan of that motivational phrase “No one is coming to save you” because I believe people show up for each other all the time – from small acts of kindness to bigger interventions. Be someone who checks in.

News.title: Angela Rayner rules out rent controls in England
News.content:
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said Prime Minister Andy Burnham is not looking at bringing in rent controls in England.

She told BBC Breakfast that changes made through the Renters' Rights Act, which came into effect in May, were "already having a significant impact on the market".

She added that controls which had been implemented in some areas of the UK over the past few years had not "necessarily brought rents down".

In 2023 when he was the mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham called for freezes to private sector rents until the cost of living crisis was over.

But Rayner told the BBC on Friday: "I don't think that rent freezes, rent controls, is a way forward at the moment.

"Three years ago, Andy called for that because there was a significant crisis in the rental market.

"We implemented between then the Renters' Rights Act which is giving renters more power and control."

Temporary rent controls were introduced in Scotland in October 2022 but expired last year.

Under new legislation, ministers in Holyrood will be able to designate certain places in Scotland as rent control areas - expected to come in by 2027.

Councils will be able to cap rent increases on some properties at a maximum of 6%.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said he wants to see rent controls brought in for all rented property in England, while Sir Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, has long called on the government to implement a cap.

The term rent controls describes a range of measures a government can implement - from capping price increases to freezing them for a period of time.

Landlord groups say they may exacerbate the housing crisis by putting owners off renting out property.

The Renters' Rights Act was brought in to give more stability and security to the 11 million people who rent from private landlords.

Under the legislation, fixed-term tenancies have been banned and it is now significantly harder for landlords to evict tenants.

Rents can also only be increased once a year to the property's "open market rent".

News.title: Fifty women tell BBC they were pressured into having sex with strangers
News.content:
Warning: This story contains details of sexual acts

Fifty women have told the BBC they were pressured or coerced by their partners into having sex with strangers.

They got in contact following an investigation which told the story of a woman who said she had been pressured into having sex with more than 100 people she did not know.

Many of the women who came forward said they had sex through swinging despite not wanting to, either because they feared the consequences of refusing or felt they had to keep their partners happy.

They spoke of deep, long-lasting trauma.

"I remember many nights of my partner keeping me up all night screaming at me, threatening me, and attempting to gaslight me into believing this was something I wanted," said one woman. "It was never what I wanted."

Another told us: "I felt like I had been given away. I felt used. I felt so dirty."

Most encounters were arranged via the website FabSwingers, say the women, which claims to have more than half a million UK active monthly accounts.

Six of the women told BBC News they had been raped by men met through the site.

One said her partner had forced her to have sex with more than 90 men through FabSwingers. On one occasion, he held her down by the ankles, she told us.

Sixteen said intimate photos of them had been uploaded to the website without their permission.

News.title: PM to spend first day working from northern branch of No 10
News.content:
Andy Burnham will hold his first meeting at the new No 10 North in Manchester later on Friday.

The branch of Downing Street in the North West will form part of the prime minister's aim to shift power from Whitehall and Westminster to regions across the country.

Ministers Lucy Powell and Louise Haigh will also operate regularly from the new site, with up to 300 civil servants expected to join them by the end of next year.

On Friday in Manchester, Burnham will chair a meeting of the National Economic Council, a cabinet committee first launched in 2008 to respond to economic challenges around the UK.

The meeting will bring together senior ministers and regional mayors to "put devolution at the centre of the government's mission to make Britain better".

Ahead of that meeting, the prime minister said: "For 40 years, power and resources have been sucked into the centre, and too many communities have felt forgotten, without the attention and investment they deserve."

He added: "The days of Whitehall resisting devolution are over, for good."

Strategic decisions about devolution and local economic growth will shift from the Treasury and the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government to No 10 North, although both departments will have input in these areas.

Angela Rayner, whose constituency is in Greater Manchester, is also expected to work from the new site for the first time on Friday.

Asked whether Burnham's messaging was too focused on the north of England, Rayner told BBC Breakfast people understood No 10 North was about driving growth in every postcode across the UK.

News.title: Hero swimmer helped two children during West Mersea beach tragedy
News.content:
Witnesses say a heroic day-tripper managed to haul two children back to shore during an incident where a mother and daughter drowned.

Beverly Smit, 60, described the unnamed rescuer swimming out to sea three times as the tragedy unfolded in West Mersea, near Colchester, on Wednesday evening.

Shally Rahman, 41, and Samiha Rahman, 15, were trying to rescue a seven-year-old boy from the water when they got into difficulty and died.

Essex Police said the group, from Barking, east London, were all related to each other and the boy remained in hospital, fighting for his life.

Recalling the moment the "Good Samaritan" sprang into action, Smit said: "They were calling for help and the children and adults were out there.

"He swam out, I think, three times. Two of the children he brought back were not in good condition.

"It's not an easy swim when the tide's coming in - you're swimming against the tide. The water [on Wednesday] was particularly quite cold."

News.title: Heat health alerts in effect for parts of UK as rain returns for some this weekend
News.content:
Yellow heat health alerts came into effect across central and southern England on Friday morning with temperatures forecast to reach 30C (86F) in places.

The alerts, issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), cover the East and West Midlands, eastern England, London, south-east England and south-west England and are valid from 09:00 BST on Friday until 09:00 on Sunday.

The UKHSA warns that heat is expected to cause minor impacts for health and social care services, with an increased risk to life for vulnerable people.

It comes as parts of the UK prepare to see much-needed rain this weekend - although amounts are expected to be relatively small, especially in the south.

A drought was officially declared for large parts of north and mid-Wales on Thursday.

The rest of Wales, along with much of central, southern and eastern England, is in "prolonged dry weather" category - one stage below a drought.

Hosepipe bans are in force for millions of customers.

News.title: UK mortgage rates rise to highest level for a month
News.content:
UK average mortgage rates have risen back to the level of a month ago as renewed tensions in the Middle East feed through to homeowners.

Lenders' funding costs have increased as markets judge that a prolonged conflict reduces the possibility of interest rate cuts by central banks.

The five biggest High Street banks are among a host of lenders which have increased their interest rates on new fixed deals in recent days.

Recent projections by the Bank of England suggest just over five million homeowners should expect their monthly mortgage repayments to increase by the end of 2028.

Mortgage rates had been falling as a ceasefire between the US and Iran initially appeared to hold.

But fresh strikes and Houthi militia attacks on oil tankers in the Red Sea reignited fears over global energy supplies.

Oil prices hit $100 a barrel for the first time since May on Thursday after several days of increases, stoking fears of higher inflation and a lower likelihood of interest rate cuts.

News.title: King's Tardis entrance as Commonwealth Games begin
News.content:
One of the louder cheers came for the Falklands Islands â in the news recently following Argentina's victory over England in the football World Cup semi-finals â and another followed when the Samoa team emerged and performed a haka in front of the dignitaries in the Royal Box.

But nothing compared to the noise which greeted the arrival of the Scotland team, who entered the arena last in their white shirts and kilts and lifted many in the capacity crowd from their seats.

A large Loch Ness Monster representation then emerged, before, backed by bagpipers and drummers, a rousing rendition of Flower of Scotland followed.

The next section of the evening featured theatrical performances â a show billed as "a love letter to Glasgow and the Commonwealth".

It began with a performance by Scottish folk and country singer Nathan Evans and a dance under a replica of Glasgow Central Station's iconic clock.

The saying "Meet me under the clock" is famous in these parts.

Singer Callum Beattie's rendition of Baccara's Yes Sir, I Can Boogie â the 1970s disco tune recently adopted as Scotland's unofficial anthem - had the Scottish athletes dancing in their seats.

Held indoors in front of about 10,000 people, this was a more intimate ceremony than the last time Glasgow hosted the Commonwealth Games, when a 40,000-strong crowd witnessed the opening of the Games in 2014 at Celtic Park.

There was a point, after the Australian state of Victoria withdrew as hosts in 2023, when some thought these Games would not happen. Glasgow stepped in at short notice to ensure otherwise.

There are eight fewer sports involved compared to 2014, given the short build-up, and venues from 12 years ago have been repurposed.

But Commonwealth Sport president Donald Rukare, wearing a tartan kilt in the colours of his home country Uganda, said this edition has been made possible by the "extraordinary legacy of 2014 and by a city that once again welcomes us with warm hearts and open arms".

News.title: Scientists find the secret of birdsong's 'spectacular diversity'
News.content:
Scientists in France say they have discovered the building blocks of the incredible diversity of birdsong.

A team analysed more than100,000 songs from 3,000 bird species and revealed that they are all composed of eight fundamental types of sound that the researchers call "motifs".

Each song, they say, is made up of combinations of these motifs - three types of trill, three types of whistle, chaotic notes and harmonies.

Birdsong is one of the natural world's most sophisticated forms of sound-based communication.

News.title: Novel analysis reveals playful side of Alan Turing
News.content:
A story written by World War Two codebreaker Alan Turing suggests he was a man with playful humour embracing his homosexuality, according to new analysis.

The six-page hand-written short story, Pryce's Buoy, has been transcribed in full for the first time and studied by Sarah Dillon, professor of literature at the University of Cambridge.

Dillon said the story offered fresh insights that challenge the view of Turing as an isolated, lonely genius.

"We've distilled a version of Turing that is a two-dimensional stereotype," she added.

Turing played a crucial role in the Allies' victory over Nazi Germany in World War Two by helping to crack codes and deciphering the infamous Enigma machine at Bletchley Park.

After the war he produced a detailed design for a digital computer in the modern sense, storing programmes in its memory.

News.title: Wildfire spotted from space as helicopter brought in to tackle blaze
News.content:
Satellite images have captured plumes of smoke and damage caused by a wildfire in north Wales.

Data gathered by BBC Verify suggests an estimated 951 hectares (2,350 acres) of the Rhinogydd mountains in Gwynedd have been burned by a wildfire that broke out earlier this month.

Nasa's satellite-based fire monitoring system has also detected heat signatures from four areas of Wales where wildfires have broken out.

It is showing heat sources at Blaenavon in Torfaen, Presteigne in Powys, and Pentre Halkyn in Flintshire.

Natural Resources Wales (NRW) said a specialist firefighting helicopter would be deployed to Rhinogydd on Friday morning after calls for "aerial support".

News.title: Southport killer Axel Rudakubana moved to psychiatric hospital
News.content:
Axel Rudakubana, who murdered three children at a dance class in Southport, has been moved from prison to a secure psychiatric hospital.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) confirmed he was transferred from HMP Belmarsh to Broadmoor, the high-security psychiatric hospital in Berkshire.

Rudakubana murdered Elsie Dot Stancombe, seven, Bebe King, six, and Alice da Silva Aguiar, nine, and injured eight other children and two adults in an attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class in July 2024.

He was given a 52-year prison sentence in January 2025 but the judge was unable to impose a whole life order due to Rudakubana being 17 when he carried out the attack. He will likely never be released.

The then Attorney-General Lord Hermer said Rudakubana's sentence was the "second-longest sentence imposed by the courts in English history".

A spokesperson for the MoJ told PA: "The families of those murdered and injured in Southport will be in this country's heart forever and our thoughts remain with them.

"Any decision to transfer an offender is made following an independent, clinical assessment, under the Mental Health Act. Following rigorous security checks, the offender has been transferred to a high-security psychiatric unit, where he will remain until assessed fit to return to prison.

"Officials have approved this transfer, on behalf of Ministers. This transfer does not change his sentence â which remains at 52 years â and of which he will serve every single day."

Under the Mental Health Act, the MoJ is likely to have had no choice but to accept doctors' recommendations about whether Rudakubana could be held safely in prison.

The law requires he be transferred back to prison when he no longer requires treatment in hospital. His sentence is not being converted into a "hospital order", which would mean he stayed at Broadmoor.

The cost of keeping Rudakubana in hospital is likely to be much higher in Broadmoor than a prison.

According to the Centre for Mental Health the average secure hospital bed costs around Â£270,000 a year.

The average cost of keeping a prisoner in Belmarsh is Â£97,740 according to figures for 2023.

In May 2025 there was an investigation after Rudakubana, now 19, allegedly attacked a prison officer with boiling water.

The Southport Public Inquiry has heard evidence about his past mental health conditions.

A senior clinician at Alder Hey Children's Hospital described his "lack of empathy" combined with a "fascination with violence" and neurodiversity, which he said added up to a "really toxic mix".

According to West London NHS Trust, Broadmoor specialises in "providing assessment, treatment and care in conditions of high security" for men.

Is is the oldest of England and Wales's three high-security hospitals and has held some of the UK's most high-profile criminals.

It was renovated in 2017 and the BBC obtained pictures from inside the hospital. They show that older prison-like cells were replaced by more spacious rooms, though still with locks on the doors.

News.title: Burnham pauses plan to release some prisoners early from September
News.content:
Andy Burnham has announced he is pausing a scheme which would have seen thousands of prisoners in England and Wales eligible to be released early.

It came after criticism of the scheme from survivors and victims' families, including the widow of PC Andrew Harper who described the possibility of his killers' early release as "deplorable".

The Sentencing Act, which was due to come into effect in September, would have seen some offenders let out at varying stages in a bid to ease prison overcrowding.

The new Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the pause aimed to "give victims and survivors certainty" and the government wanted to make sure it got "the implementation of this policy right".

He added a review would also look at the information given to survivors and victims' families as part of the early release process.

Burnham earlier said: "No prisoners will be let out under this policy until we have conducted an urgent review and done everything we can to minimise risk to the public."

He added: "Where changes are needed, we will not hesitate to make them."

Under the act, some offenders would have been let out after serving a third of their sentence, rather than half.

The rest of their sentence would be spent in the community, where they would be monitored and could be returned to prison if they offended again.

More serious offenders would have been released after serving half of their sentence, rather than two-thirds.

The policy was brought in to ease overcrowding in the prison system but has been criticised by opposition parties, as well as victims and their families.

The scheme would have seen around 700 prisoners released in early September, the BBC understands.

The decision to pause the scheme came after criticism from the family of Thames Valley Police officer Andrew Harper, who was killed in Berkshire in 2019 when he was dragged by a car down a country road by three teenagers.

Two of the killers of PC Harper, who were both sentenced to 13 years in prison, would have benefited from the scheme from June 2027, when the longest fixed sentences would have been added to the scheme.

PC Harper's widow, Lissie, called the plans "deplorable" and said politicians were "making decisions from behind a desk that will have real and lasting consequences" for the families of victims.

His mother, meanwhile, said her son had not been given "proper justice" and "every victim will be feeling the same" about the early prison release scheme.

Thousands of letters had been sent to victims in recent weeks, warning them that the early release scheme was coming in September.

Norris, who voted in support of the Sentencing Act under Starmer's government, later said the decision to pause was made after "listening to victims" and he hoped to provide them "certainty as soon as we can".

He said: "The prime minister and I have heard from victims and survivors and from people across the country about their concerns about the implementation of some very important elements of the Sentencing Act."

One element the government needed to get right was the information provided to victims before prisoners were released, Norris added.

Norris refused to be drawn on why he did not raise concerns when the Sentencing Act was first introduced but said Burnham was "quite right" to review the scheme.

Jade Belgrove, a survivor of sexual assault who has been campaigning against the early release scheme, said it was "such a relief that we've been heard".

She told BBC News that when she received a letter informing her that her attacker might be released early "it was horrific".

Belgrove said it even led her to question whether reporting the assault in the first place was worth it.

News.title: UK complacent about war threat, warns BAE boss
News.content:
The UK has been too complacent about the risk of foreign attack, the boss of Europe's biggest defence contractor BAE Systems has warned.

Dr Charles Woodburn told the BBC in an exclusive interview that the level of threat was the highest he'd seen in his lifetime.

He welcomed the recent boost to defence spending but said much more would be needed to hit the government's commitment to spend 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035.

He also warned we were not far from the use of autonomous lethal weapons by countries that may not follow the UK's policy of maintaining human control.

In a rare interview, Woodburn told the BBC the reality of modern warfare had "changed quite profoundly" and that UK defence spending had to change with it.

He said Russia and Ukraine had become "incredibly adept" at using autonomy in the form of drones and counter drones.

"It's something that we now have to really understand and make sure that we're able to provide the capabilities that can counter that and deter aggression," he said.

News.title: Rayner rules out repaying severance cash after making cabinet return
News.content:
A lump sum, equivalent of 25% of the annual ministerial salary, is payable when a minister stops holding office. Departing ministers who are aged over 65 or are reappointed within three weeks do not qualify.

The 2025/26 accounts, external for the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government record the severance payment for Rayner.

In her first interview since returning to government, Rayner was pressed on whether she would return the money.

She told Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5 Live: "No, my severance payment was given to me at the time, I had worked in government for a period of time and then I came out of government for just under a year."

She added: "I will be delivering in government again."

Rayner earlier said her criticism of the Conservatives over severance payments came at a time when there was a "revolving door" which saw ministers return to government "after 40-odd days".

The Conservatives earlier this week said Rayner had "quit in disgrace and took a Â£17k payout" last year.

The party added: "Now she's got her old job back, will she return the cash? Or is it one rule for Labour, and another for everyone else?"

Rayner's departure last September came after the prime minister's ethics adviser, Sir Laurie Magnus, said she had "acted with integrity" but concluded that she had breached the ministerial code.

Sir Laurie said she did get legal advice when buying the property, but failed to seek further expert tax advice as recommended.

In May, Rayner resolved her tax affairs with HMRC following an investigation, settling Â£40,000 in unpaid stamp duty.

The MP for Ashton-under-Lyne said she had been "exonerated" of the accusation that she had "deliberately sought to avoid tax".

Rayner told Matt Chorley: "The situation I went through last year was really difficult, it was difficult for my family, but I felt I'd let people down and I never want to let people down, I want to fight for them."

Rayner also said she has "unfinished business" in government, including on building council houses and supporting local government.

Burnham has said he wants to deliver "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period".

Asked for details to explain what this will look like, Rayner said she would not provide an "exact figure" or provide a date for when she considers the post-war period to have ended.

She said: "We want to aspire to get as far as possible and what we've done as a government is put more investment in that, the Â£39bn for social and affordable housing grant funding that we want to get out the door."

News.title: Mum and daughter who died at beach were trying to save boy, 7
News.content:
A woman and her 15-year-old daughter who died after getting into difficulty in the water on the Essex coast were trying to help a seven-year-old boy, police have said.

The child remains in a critical condition in hospital after the incident at West Mersea, near Colchester, on Wednesday evening. Three others were taken to hospital.

The victims have been named by a family member as Shally Rahman, 41, and teenager Samiha Rahman. Police said all the people involved knew each other.

Shally's brother-in-law Matiur Rahman said the family was enjoying a seaside holiday when a "big wave came and took them".

"My whole family, we are, like, speechless," said Matiur Rahman, who used to live in Bradford, but spoke to the BBC from Bangladesh.

"We are very shocked. We can't explain [what has happened]."

He said his niece was a "very, very good person" and his sister-in-law was "a very helpful person".

News.title: Gary Lineker among millionaires asking Andy Burnham to tax them more
News.content:
Millionaires including former footballer Gary Lineker and music producer Brian Eno have written to new prime minister Andy Burnham asking to be taxed more.

In an open letter, 120 well-off Britons told Burnham: "We can afford it. We're not talking about higher taxes on those who get up and go to work for their income every day, but on the very richest whose income is derived from the wealth they hold."

Organised by Patriotic Millionaires, the letter said it would lead to a more equal society, and urged a "devolution of wealth and power from the very richest".

People can already give money or stocks voluntarily to the Treasury using a donation facility.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Lineker is "very welcome to pay more tax he can write a cheque to the Treasury, no one is stopping him."

Patriotic Millionaires support a 2% tax on wealth over Â£10m.

"Millionaires are a patriotic bunch," the letter states. "We love this country and we want it to succeed.

"But success requires investment and a primary source of untouched capital investment is sitting with us, in untaxed potential."

Other signatories include Richard Curtis, who wrote the film Notting Hill, and Ian Gregg, the former managing director of Greggs and son of the bakery chain's founder. Scottish crime writer Val McDermid and former financial trader-turned-equality campaigner Gary Stevenson also signed the letter.

Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds said she would welcome UK millionaires increasing the amount of tax they pay but said any major changes would be announced during a Budget.

"I welcome the fact that people of good means are saying that they want to pay more. They can pay more," she said and pointed to the Treasury's donation link.

The renewed call for higher tax on the wealthy follows a similar campaign in previous years.

Burnham did not rule out a wealth tax when asked about it by Lineker - formerly the BBC's highest paid presenter - a few days before he became prime minister.

He suggested he may have "to ask for a little more" tax at some point.

Lineker was paid around Â£1.3m a year before he left the BBC. He is worth a reported Â£30m.

In 2023, Lineker won his appeal against HMRC over a Â£4.9m tax bill, after the UK tax authority pursued him over taxes on income from both the BBC and BT Sport, from 2013 to 2014, and 2017 to 2018.

The latest call from Patriotic Millionaires said there is a "need to embrace a new kind of devolution of wealth and power, from the very richest in order to reinvest back into our greatest asset in every region".

It added that in its own poll, the majority of millionaires wanted a higher tax on themselves.

"There are a few people left with outdated economic thinking and few others desperate to hold onto every penny they can... Those that can't see past the end of their own self interest have no place in designing a Britain for the future," the letter said.

Musician Brian Eno told BBC Radio Lincolnshire the tax system was "very generous to rich people".

"If you're wealthy you don't pay very much tax but hire a clever bunch of accountants who somehow get you off that," he said.

He also dismissed the idea that lots of millionaires would leave the UK if they were taxed too much.

Tyson Fury will return to the ring today, boxing in a warm-up bout for his long-awaited fight against Anthony Joshua.

In Thailand, where Fury has been training throughout the past year, the British heavyweight will face ex-world-title challenger Mariusz Wach, one day before Joshua fights Kristian Prenga in Saudi Arabia.

Should Fury and his “AJ” win these contests, they will finally clash towards the end of this year, with a November showdown at Wembley Stadium possible – if the fight begins in the early hours of the morning, apparently.

open image in gallery Tyson Fury after outpointing Arslanbek Makhmudov in April ( PA )

Some might say that Fury, 37, has already had a warm-up for his planned fight with Joshua; in April, Fury ended his fifth retirement and outpointed Arslanbek Makhmudov in Tottenham. But the former world heavyweight champion wants to go again, facing Wach in a fight whose proceeds will go to charity, according to Fury.

The big question, however, is if fans can watch the fight at all... Here’s all you need to know:

When is the fight?

Fury vs Wach will take place on Friday 24 July at Max Muaythai Stadium in Pattaya, Thailand. The main card is believed to begin at 3.15pm BST (7.15am PT / 9.15am CT / 10.15am ET), with main-event ring walks then likely at 5pm BST (9am PT / 11am CT / 12pm ET).

How can I watch it?

Fury has said: “This great fight will not be streamed live! It will only be broadcast on my hit Netflix TV show ‘At Home With The Furys’ season three.” There is currently no release date for that season. The Independent will provide live updates from the event, however.

The recent heatwaves have left some wishing the unbearable heat away and dreaming of getaways in subzero temperatures surrounded by mounds of snow.

Thoughts of après fondues and cosy chalets come to mind, as well as time spent out on the slopes with your family before all huddling around the fire with hot chocolates in the evening. If these images are making you long for the ski season to arrive, it might be time to plan a family ski holiday to a child-friendly resort in Andorra, Finland and Slovakia in the next winter break.

There are plenty of ways the whole family can enjoy a ski holiday if they head to resorts with gentle terrain, wide nursery runs and patient ski schools that help little legs to get the hang of the slopes their first few times around. Plenty of resorts also have more challenging pistes for the experienced skiers in the group.

Skiing can be a pricey pursuit, so it often helps to book in advance and take advantage of early-bird discounts. Here are the family-friendly winter destinations that toddlers, teens and in-betweens will love, to inspire your next ski holiday with the whole clan.

1. Les Contamines, France

open image in gallery At the foot of Mont Blanc, Les Contamines is a dream for beginners ( Photos by Getty )

Best for: Budget breaks

At the foot of Mont Blanc, Les Contamines is a quiet and traditional resort with 120km of varied slopes above 1,200m altitude, suitable for all abilities of skiers. Families will particularly enjoy the dedicated beginners areas at the Loyers and Nivorin slopes, Ludopark fun runs and evening snowshoe outings. For the smallest members of the family, there is a nursery for infants aged two to four, with activities including throwing snowballs, while there are six ski schools in the resort for those who are just starting out. Families can choose from hotels, short-term lets, gites, mountain refuges and campsites to stay in.



2. St Johann, Austria

open image in gallery Tirol’s St Johann has first-class ski schools and family-friendly snowparks to entertain the whole clan ( Getty )

Best for: Family-friendly chalets

There are 210km of groomed pistes and toboggan rides awaiting broods visiting the alluring St Johann resort, 60km from Salzburg. Think famed schnitzel at cosy huts, slopes for both seasoned and shaky skiers and the tranquil family area of Hahnbaum in this enchanting Austrian Tirol ski destination. Off-piste, Murmi’s Kinderland indoor playground, indoor climbing walls at Koasa Boulder and water slides at Panorama Badewelt promise to entertain little ones.



Andermatt, Switzerland​

open image in gallery Fun slopes and toboggan runs make Andermatt a skiing wonderland for kids ( Getty )

Best for: Off-piste fun

Andermatt’s fun slopes, toboggan runs and slope-side family car parks make the rising Swiss ski resort a wonderland for groups with children. The Andermatt+Sedrun+Disentis area offers a welcome range of blue slopes for beginners with plenty of gentle terrain. Traditional wooden chalets meet luxury hotels in the town’s centre and – midway up the Gütsch-Express cable car – the Matti Family Paradise outdoor playground offers endless hours of fun on swings, peak-inspired climbing walls and slides.



3. Soldeu, Andorra

open image in gallery Soldeu’s ski school and hotel kids clubs are great for a family break ( Getty )

Best for: Ski schools

A family trip to Soldeu, Andorra’s largest ski area, features 210km of slopes easily accessible for all ages, including a dedicated “Snow Garden”, an enclosed area for children between three and five years old to play in the snow. The main schools in Soldeu are run by snow sports organisation Grandvalira, which offers English-speaking instructors for group and private lessons, as well as a nursery drop-off service at the top of the gondolas for Snow Garden visits, storytelling and games. The tree-lined valley’s relaxed atmosphere and quaint accommodation will suit holidaymakers with little ones, and kids under six fine-tuning their ski skills are entitled to free lift passes across the ski area.



4. Ruka, Finland

open image in gallery The Rosa & Rudolf Family Park in Ruka features wide slopes, six magic carpets and a tubing hill ( Getty )

Best for: Winter activities

A winter wonderland for the whole family, Ruka in northern Finland sees 200 days of snow blanketed across 24km of slopes and 100km of cross-country skiing trails. The Rosa & Rudolf Family Park features wide slopes, six magic carpet beginner ski lifts and a tubing hill, complete with charming elf houses and an outdoor fireplace for grilling sausages. Skiing aside, a Ruka itinerary includes snowmobiling, husky sledging, Northern Light hunting and reindeer sleigh rides for guaranteed festive fun at Christmas.



5. Jasna, Slovakia

open image in gallery Slovakia’s largest ski resort, Jasna, offers gentle blues and family-run inns off-piste ( Getty )

Best for: Great-value skiing

Jasna, Slovakia’s largest ski resort, and in the Tatra Mountains, has 50km of steady slopes running down two sides of Mount Chopok for a great-value classic ski getaway. Easy pistes, peaks above 2,500m and affordable bowls of spicy goulash at slope-side restaurants make the Slovakian ski resort an inviting destination for families. A fenced area, Maxiland, also offers safe skiing for children and beginners away from more experienced skiers.



6. Beaver Creek, Colorado, USA

open image in gallery Beaver Creek’s McCoy and Red Buffalo ski parks have dedicated learning spaces for little ones ( Getty )

Best for: An American adventure

Beaver Creek in Colorado’s Rocky Mountains has a relaxed rhythm of gentle glade runs, rolling forest pistes and sun-soaked on-slope restaurants. Picture cruising down blues that all abilities will enjoy, wood-fringed nursery slopes and an efficient lift network connecting the total 150km of slopes, all complemented by luxury lodgings. Better still, come Christmas, torchlight parades, sleigh rides and twinkling ice rinks greet visitors to Beaver Creek – you can even expect a visit from Santa.



Abruzzo, Italy

open image in gallery Beginners’ slopes in Abruzzo offer the Italian ski experience away from the crowds of the Alps ( Getty )

Best for: La dolce vita

The Abruzzo region, to the east of Rome, boasts not only the almost-3,000m peaks of the Apennine Mountains and a pretty solid snow record, but a ski season from December to April that welcomes families for half the price of some of the big-name resorts in the Italian Alps and Dolomites. Beginner slopes in Aremogna offer wide blue runs while the beginner’s ski school area at the base of Roccaraso-Pizzalto teaches youngsters technique, safety and how to master the dreaded button lift.

A major archaeological site in the West Bank and a set of castles in southern Lebanon will be listed as World Heritage sites, despite objections from Israel.

The decision at a U.N. Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization meeting in South Korea came days after Israel's Foreign Ministry urged the committee to reject efforts to designate the small West Bank town of Sebastia and the Lebanese castles, calling the nominations a "weaponization of cultural heritage."

At their meeting in Busan, members of the UNESCO committee decided to place Sebastia and five castles in Lebanon's Mount Amel area on both the World Heritage List and the List of World Heritage in Danger after reviewing the nominations on an emergency basis.

Sebastia, a hilltop town about 10 kilometers (6 miles) northwest of Nablus in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, is identified by scholars as ancient Samara, capital of the biblical Kingdom of Israel. The area's archaeological remains span the Iron Age, Roman, Byzantine and Islamic periods. Christian and Islamic tradition holds that John the Baptist was buried there, according to a UNESCO website.

open image in gallery Israeli settlers are pictured near Israeli military vehicles during an official visit by a group of foreign diplomats accredited by the Palestinian Authority at the archaeological site of Sebastia, north of Nablus in the occupied West Bank, on June 29, 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

Sebastia's nomination, first submitted by the Palestinian delegation to UNESCO in 2012, argued that World Heritage status was needed to help preserve the site, saying it remains largely undeveloped under Israeli control and requires additional conservation despite attracting tourists.

The designation comes as Israel, which does not recognize a Palestinian state, moves to expropriate large swaths of land around the site, even as it faces pressure to crack down on violence by Israeli settlers in the Palestinian territory.

The five castles in the Mount Amel region are recognized for their layered architectural heritage, combining Crusader, Ayyubid, Mamluk and local influences, reflecting the evolution of fortified architecture over nearly nine centuries, according to a UNESCO description.

In Tuesday's statement, Israel's Foreign Ministry accused the Palestinian delegation of waging a "hostile, one-sided campaign" at UNESCO by falsely portraying Sebastia as an area facing an emergency, calling the effort a political attempt to "erase the site's profound, well-documented Jewish and Christian history."

open image in gallery Smoke rises to the sky in an area near Beaufort Castle following an Israeli military strike in southern Lebanon as seen from northern Israel, Friday, June 19, 2026. (AP Photo/Leo Correa, File) ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

Israel withdrew from UNESCO in 2019, accusing the organization of being biased against it and of downplaying its historical ties to the Holy Land.

Israel's Foreign Ministry also took objection to efforts to list Beaufort Castle in southern Lebanon as a World Heritage site. The castle was part of the nomination covering five castles in the Mount Amel area.

The ministry said Hezbollah, an Iran-backed militant group, has turned Beaufort Castle into a military stronghold by building tunnels beneath the site and launching rockets from the area, and accused UNESCO of ignoring those developments.

UNESCO and the Lebanese embassy in South Korea declined to comment on the Israeli claims about Hezbollah.

The UNESCO committee on Wednesday placed another Lebanese site, Tyre, an ancient Phoenician city in the southern part of the country, on the list of world heritage sites in danger.
