World.title: Friends turned millionaires take tech company shares battle to court
World.content:
The millionaire co-founder of an Australian video tech company behind some of Hollywood's biggest blockbusters has told the Federal Court a decade of hostility by fellow shareholders has unfairly barred him from selling his lucrative stake in the billion-dollar business.

Peter Barber is suing the company he helped establish, Blackmagic Design, and co-founders Grant Petty and Douglas Clarke over claims he has been denied dividends for years, access to information about the business, and the ability to sell his shares.

Mr Barber, now based in Singapore, also claims Mr Petty sabotaged an attempted investment in the company that valued Blackmagic at as much as $1.5 billion.

Lawyers for Peter Barber told the court he effectively has around $98 million in assets locked up in the company. (LinkedIn: Peter Barber)

Blackmagic has grown rapidly since it was founded in Melbourne in 2001 by Mr Barber and Mr Petty, old high school friends who grew up in Shepparton, and Mr Clarke, whom Mr Petty reportedly met at an Apple user group.

Last financial year the company generated more than $550 million in revenue and now operates 10 offices worldwide.

The tech juggernaut is in high demand by both amateur content creators and US production houses which used its video editing software DaVinchi Resolve for box office smash Avatar, the recent Peaky Blinders film, and hit television series Grey's Anatomy and Yellowstone.

The company's hardware was also behind 2019's The Lion King and Avengers: Age of Ultron.

Blackmagic Design's video editing software DaVinchi Resolve Studio was used for post-production on Yellowstone. (Paramount)

Selling shares would 'destroy the place'

Court documents seen by the ABC show Mr Barber first floated the idea of selling his 28 per cent stake in the company a decade ago when his professional relationship with Mr Petty broke down.

A statement of claim filed by Mr Barber alleges Mr Petty said he would "fight back" against shares sold to a third party, and promised to be "the most hostile f***ing agent you can possibly imagine".

"[I'm] not gonna assist in any way your selling your shares," Mr Petty allegedly told Mr Barber in a 2016 phone call.

"I'm simply not gonna do that because it's gonna f***ing destroy the place."

A few months later the 56-year-old was ousted from Blackmagic's board of directors when the company told corporate watchdog ASIC that Mr Barber had failed to perform his executive duties.

He claims that since then he has not received a salary and that dividends have gone unpaid without explanation since 2022 while the company's remaining directors and other key personnel have been compensated millions of dollars each year.

Lawyers for Mr Barber told the Federal Court on Thursday their client effectively has around $98 million in assets locked up in the company.

Peter Barber is asking the court to order Mr Petty and Mr Clarke to buy out his share, facilitate the sale, or wind up the company. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

According to the documents, venture capital firm Five V Capital had expressed interest in investing in Blackmagic after assessing the company at between $900 million and $1.5 billion.

It pulled out after being told Mr Petty would not entertain a sale.

Mr Petty, Blackmagic's CEO, and Mr Clarke have been contacted for comment through their lawyers who are due to file a defence to the claims next month.

The court heard the pair are considering making an application which could require Mr Barber to set aside a sum of money to pay their legal costs should his case fail.

Mr Barber was last year appointed CEO and managing director of Atomos, another Australian video tech outfit, which on Friday responded to media reporting about the proceedings.

"[The proceedings] have no impact on Atomos, its operations, strategy, financial position or governance, and no impact on Mr Barber's ability to perform his duties," Atomos said in an announcement to the ASX.

Mr Barber is asking the court to order Mr Petty and Mr Clarke – who each own 35.8 per cent of Blackmagic — to buy out his share in the company, facilitate the sale to a third party, or wind up the company entirely.

The matter will return to court next month.

World.title: Have the AFL's rule changes worked? Not exactly
World.content:
There is nothing more constant than change.

People have argued about the future of football for as long as the game has existed.

Every year players, fans and football staffers await the new direction or interpretations handed down from high.

Some changes are winners and stand the test of time — such as the 50 metre arc and the centre square.

Others are destined for the dustbin of history, such as the flick pass and around the ground bounces.

Regardless, change is never far from sporting administrators of different codes and sports. The AFL is not immune from this want to improve the sport.

Rule changes among what's new in the AFL for 2026 The new AFL season is only days away, and there are plenty of new things to get your head around. Get up to speed before Thursday night's opener.

Ahead of the 2026 season seven rule changes and interpretation shifts were heralded as being common sense solutions to perceived long-standing problems surrounding the sport.

Changes to the centre bounce, kick-ins, shrugs, the "stand" rule and last disposal out of bounds were implemented. Some elements of the footy fan base were excited by the changes, others horrified.

"We have consulted clubs and other industry stakeholders over the past six months and taken on board their feedback and ideas, and we believe these changes will make a positive impact on the game," AFL executive general manager Football Performance Greg Swann said before the commencement of the season.

The aims of each change were varied but aligned to increase scoring, reduce game time and improve the look and feel of the game.

So far scoring has increased about 3.5 points per game compared to last year.

Scoreboard operators haven't been this busy since the 2017 season, with early season scoring rates threatening to push the clock back even further.

But that number alone may not tell the whole story.

With the season winding towards finals, research undertaken by the ABC and Andrew Whelan of Wheelo Ratings looks at whether the changes have had their intended impact.

Centring the truth

Rule changes around centre ball-ups have increased the numbers of ruckmen leaping for the ball. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

To the casual fan there were few more iconic parts of the Australian game than the centre bounce. The biggest optical change to the game in 2026 was the removal of the centre bounce and changes to how rucks engaged at the restart.

The bounce had been the start of each game since its formal introduction in 1887.

For many the bounce was integral to the look and feel of the sport — a unique element that set the native code away from the other global codes of football.

AFL rule change injury fears Geelong's Shannon Neale might have escaped a serious injury, but coaches and players are beginning to voice concerns the AFL's rule changes could lead to more rucks getting hurt.

But it had become untenable in the face of umpire injuries and skill barriers, seen to reduce the ranks of vital recruits.

"Currently, umpire pathways are being narrowed by the requirement of the bounce. By removing the skill aspect of bouncing the ball, umpires can focus their energy on adjudicating the game and consistency of decision-making," Swann stated.

At the same time that they removed the bounce, the league also instituted a change to encourage more rucks to leap at centre ball-ups.

According to the AFL, just 21 per cent of centre bounce ruck contests had at least one ruck leaping last year. That's down from about two-thirds just two years prior.

After the preseason Swann was keen to sell the success of both changes.

"The unintended consequences from a good perspective is scores out of the centre bounces have gone up. It's a very small sample size, but the things that we wanted — the game length has gone back, the scoring has gone up, scoring from centre bounces has gone up, so we're hopeful that goes into the season proper as well."

At face value the rule changes — in combination — have delivered in spades. Scoring from centre bounces are at their highest level for at least 20 years.

Digging a little deeper presents more questions as to its impact.

While scoring is up from centre bounces, the major reason why they are up is a little more unconventional.

Instead of fast flowing play from the restart the biggest contributor to the jump are scores from free kicks.

Free kicks at the restart have surged in 2026, perhaps sparked by confusion around the new rules.

More points are being put on the scoreboard from these free kicks than in recent years.

Instead of the dynamic future promised from the new ruck set up, the reality is more of the same buttressed by a surge in indiscretions.

With more centre ball-ups overall, teams are scoring 0.96 points per live ball centre clearance, up just 0.02 points per clearance on last year.

There's also been a subtle tactical evolution as the season has progressed.

As teams have become accustomed to the new rules, scoring from centre bounce has also dropped.

The predictable new ball-up has become easier to defend as winter has gone deeper and teams have become better equipped at limiting damage from the middle.

In the last five weeks teams have averaged just 10.6 points per game from the middle — a big drop on the fast start to the year and the past three full seasons.

While centre bounce scoring is up about 12 per cent on last season, it still only makes up around 14.5 per cent of all scoring. That's only 1 per cent more than the contribution last year.

Teams are better at getting the ball inside 50 from centre bounces this year than years past however, contributing to the territory game so important to many teams.

While rule changes often take a season or two to fully bed down, it appears the early optimism for increased centre restart scoring may be diminishing.

The new centre bounce revolution may be more a minor change in the grand scheme of football things.

Where do I stand?

Far more contentious has been the introduction of the "stand" rule six years ago.

For a sizeable cohort of fans across the league it is the single most hated rule in the AFL rule book.

Some of the rule changes have allowed teams to move the ball easier with limits on defenders' encroachment. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Designed to anchor the mark to a single spot, and prevent the creep of defenders, it aimed to open up aggressive ball use into the middle of the ground.

This year the rule has been slightly tightened to prevent a nearby player retreating "outside 5", instead requiring them to remain in place or to head to the actual spot of the mark or free kick.

Since 2021, many have attributed improved transition success from defence to the new rule. The accepted wisdom is that there has been at least a small improvement in the ability to move the ball due to 'stand'.

This trend has continued through 2026 so far, with a bump in both categories so far. But much like the centre bounce successes, there's more than meets the eye initially.

The increase in transition from defence to attack is largely down to stoppage and kick-in transitions. This matters because these areas are less impacted — or not impacted at all — by the 'stand' rule.

Teams usually escape the contest via broken (not set) play from stoppages.

The 'stand' rule has the biggest impact in set play in the back half of the ground. With the ball already entering in pressurised general play, the 'stand' rule has a far smaller impact on play than in the intercept game — if it has any real impact at all.

The rise in kick-in transition is even more fascinating to consider.

The introduction of a reduced time limit for restarting play has seemingly led teams to becoming more aggressive when bringing the ball back in after a behind.

With teams taking more direct kick-ins, there is more risk of defence's being caught if the ball is turned over. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Matt Roberts)

The average length of kick-ins is about 3 metres longer in 2026 than three years ago. Kick in targets have also gone more central, with about 40 per cent this year heading up the corridor versus about 25 per cent in 2023.

This has led to a rise in full field transition, and an increased risk of the ball going back the other way.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

By contrast, the ability to move the ball after intercepting has actually declined from last year.

Despite a rash of teams focusing on overlap handball, the overall trend has seen a decline in success of this type of movement.

There's also been a slight decline overall in the ability to move the ball from defensive 50 to the front half of the ground.

This is usually seen as the break-even success measure for teams to achieve in transition.

While the changes to 'stand' may look dramatic, the ability for defenders to trail overlap runners has not changed, nor has the ability for sides to zone off defensively up the ground.

Many of the scintillating highlights that are attributed to stand are more down to poor defending than the "intrusive" new rule.

What hasn't changed dramatically is the number of 50m penalties called due to stand infractions, or general unhappiness with the rule from some quarters of football fandom.

For these people, the only solution is complete overhaul.

In the balance the reality probably sits somewhere in the middle — not truly transformative, nor game destroying.

Stopping the stoppages

This season also brings about a radical change to the game's out of bounds laws. Following the lead of the SANFL and AFLW, the league introduced a "last disposal" rule to encourage play through the corridor and away from the boundaries.

The rule provides a free kick to the opposition where a side clearly disposes the ball via kick or handball before it passes over the boundary line — regardless of intent or whether it is on the full.

The impact of this rule change has been clear — but again with an interesting caveat.

Throw-ins are unsurprisingly down, with approximately five fewer boundary umpire overheads per game. Far more surprising is the drop in ball-ups per game.

The number of around the ground ball-ups has fallen by almost the same amount as throw ins.

The effect for both is quite dramatic through the middle of the ground. For the first time since the start of COVID there have been more stoppages in each arc than outside them.

This has led to individual stoppages being more threatening than ever before.

But as a result of the reduced volume, the stoppage game has also contributed less to the overall scoreboard than ever.

The intercept game remains the bedrock of football, despite the focus of media and fans on the dead-ball contest.

This reduction in stoppages has likely had the biggest impact on the reduction of game time.

Around two and a half minutes on average, or about two minutes on median, has been reduced from game lengths in 2026.

While better than nothing, for most fans this difference would barely be noticeable.

Next changes up?

While length of games is the hot topic of conversation, there is still more to do in trying to prevent head knocks and concussions. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Jason McCawley)

Already focus has begun to turn to the next wave of rule changes.

Chief amongst them is the length of the game.

"We've knocked off 3 minutes per game but is it enough? Probably not," Swann told Channel 7 this week.

More radical options have been tabled to further reduce game time. The most radical of these appears to be a reduction in the length of games to 16 or 18 minutes plus time on — similar to the COVID-impacted 2020 season.

This would likely occur when the league expands its home and away schedule to 24 games per team once Tasmania enters the competition in 2028.

Such a change is popular amongst many football people, but is a harder sell to a cynical and change-fatigued public.

"The COVID quarter (length) felt about right. Now maybe (that's) too short — I don't know. But it keeps the game close. You know I think we want close games," GWS coach Adam Kingsley told the ABC earlier this year.

Kingsley is far from alone in this desire, with premiership coaches Chris Fagan and Chris Scott — as well as former AFLPA president Patrick Dangerfield — calling for similar reforms in previous years.

The unspoken part of these continuous sets of rule changes and interpretation amendments are the bigger fish that are yet to be fried.

For too long the AFL have seemingly been unwilling to substantially address the elephant in the room — that of player safety and head trauma.

For example, when introducing the changes to the ruck engagement rule, Greg Swann was clear about the risks, specifically around PCL injuries to rucks.

"I think you'd be naive to say it's not going to happen — it'll happen," Swann acknowledged at the start of the year.

"If there was a pandemic of them you might change it back."

This approach appears to run contrary to much of the rhetoric around the importance of player safety in the modern game.

When limits to run up and changes of engagement at centre bounces were originally introduced they were backed by a robust base of evidence including academic research.

Instead of leaning on this, the league appears to be throwing caution to the wind for little real gain.

As a whole, injuries still are prevalent across the league, and still often affect the best of the best.

This carries through to the biggest challenge currently facing the sport.

There is still an uneasy tension between the potential for traumatic brain injuries to occur as a result of the sport that players and fans love and the enjoyment of the sport itself.

The AFL and clubs are facing class action suits over past responses to these risks.

As of next season clubs will have mandated limits around contact training following a recommendation from the Victoria State Coroner's inquest into the death of former AFL player Shane Tuck in 2023.

In that inquest the AFL provided a submission that they were considering a limitation at that time as to be guided by medical evidence.

That inquest recommended that the AFL should implement contact training rule restrictions by the commencement of the 2025 AFL/W preseason.

These rules are still yet to come into force.

While there has been a focus on training, there are also the on-field rule-based elements that seemingly have not been publicly considered by recent administrations.

Since the AFL changed the "prior opportunity" element of the holding the ball rule to better reward tacklers in 1996 the number of tackles per game has increased sharply.

In this time there has been a sharp rise in tackles per game and direct contact pressure. Tackle coaches have been introduced across the league, and an intense focus developed on locking the ball in during tackles.

In addition, the evolution of the game has meant that there is an increase of contested marking events — particularly with a third or fourth player present to spoil the ball.

Prior research funded by Monash University and the AFL suggests that these two situations account for the vast majority of head acceleration events in a game of football.

This research suggests that men's AFL players face 5.7 head acceleration events per game, and women's players 3 per game, on average. While this is less than other sports such as American football and rugby union, a reduction of these events should be a priority for the league.

Until these issues are substantively addressed the biggest need for reform will still be on the table, while much of the football landscape is inundated by relatively benign, minor changes.

One can hope that commonsense can be found soon.

World.title: Court win for Islamic school principal clears way for return to job
World.content:
A New South Wales school principal at the centre of an investigation over alleged antisemitic comments could resume his role after a court ruling in his favour.

Sheikh Abdulghani Albaf took the NSW Education Standards Authority (NESA) and the education minister to court over a finding earlier this year that he did not "meet the fit and proper requirements" of being principal of the New Madinah College at Young.

The Supreme Court has ruled he was not granted procedural fairness during an investigation of alleged antisemitic comments on social media.

Sheikh Albaf's lawyer Stephen Blanks said his client welcomed the ruling.

"The court is absolutely correct in saying the committee failed to discharge its duties appropriately," he said.

"He gave an undertaking in January, well before NESA's decision, that he will not make any further social media posts and he's complied with that undertaking.

" Sheikh Albaf hopes he can now return to his position as principal of New Madinah College and continue his positive work with the school. "

The finding came after a lengthy investigation by NESA into the K-10 school, which teaches students the Koran, the Arabic language and Islamic values as well as core subjects.

It followed a 2025 investigation by the NSW and federal education departments into comments about Zionism made over several years from an account bearing the name of Sheikh Albaf.

In February NESA informed the school it risked being deregistered if it did not remove Sheikh Albaf from his position.

New Madinah College at Young is an Islamic kindergarten to year 10 school. (ABC News: Andrew Mangelsdorf )

In her judgement, Acting Justice Monika Schmidt AM found Sheikh Albaf had been denied procedural fairness by NESA and its Registration and Accreditation Committee because it did not disclose its findings and provide him an opportunity to be heard prior to adopting them.

"I have concluded the Committee’s determination must be set aside, it will have to revisit its determination in light of all the relevant information it receives," she said.

"If the result of its further decision-making process is a recommendation to the Minister that the College’s registration be cancelled, because Sheikh Albaf is not a fit and proper person, both he and the College will have a right to pursue a review of that decision."

Sheikh Albaf stood himself down from his role as the school's principal in January this year.

Acting Justice Schmidt noted that Sheikh Albaf remained in that position but was no longer being paid by the college, and that a decision about his ongoing employment was paused while the legal proceedings were being heard.

She noted that NESA's investigation followed enquiries it received from the media about Sheikh Albaf after the December 2025 Bondi attack.

Her findings also noted "the Sheikh does accept that he should not have used intemperate language, as he did in some of his posts".

In a statement to the ABC, a NESA spokesperson said it acknowledged today's judgement by the NSW Supreme Court.

The director the New Madinah College board has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Defence minister confirms former senior naval officer faces court martial
World.content:
Defence Minister Richard Marles has confirmed that a former senior naval officer is facing a court martial, although a military court has ordered their identity remain suppressed.

Australian daily digital newspaper The Nightly reported earlier this week that the former officer is facing charges connected to "lucrative military contracts" awarded in Western Australia.

It is not clear exactly when the alleged wrongdoing occurred, but The Nightly reported the matters under investigation took place before the Albanese government won power in 2022.

The former officer will face eight charges in a military trial set down for up to six weeks from September 14 in front of Judge Advocate Major General Michael Cowen.

Michael Cowen will hear the case in the military court. (Facebook: Australian Honours and Rewards)

One defence source confirmed to the ABC that the former officer held a senior position within the military hierarchy.

But the judge advocate has issued a non-publication order suppressing their name, saying the accused should be referred to only under a pseudonym: "Star Ranked Officer in the Royal Australian Navy, Officer Brown".

A "star ranked officer" refers to the senior ranks of the navy, which includes vice-admirals, rear-admirals and commodores.

The Department of Defence has also declined to provide details about the case because of legal and privacy obligations.

Military tribunal 'appropriate' setting for case, minister says

Mr Marles was asked this morning if it was appropriate for the matter to be handled by a military tribunal rather than a civilian court, which is more open to the public.

"The answer … is that is appropriate," he told reporters in Adelaide.

"But because this is now in a legal process there's not much I can really add to this, in a public way.

"We now let those processes play out."

And when he was asked if he was alarmed by the development, Mr Marles repeated that the legal process should be allowed to "play out".

"A court martial is a legal process. So it's important that play out," he said.

"And I think that should play out without commentary from me."

David Shoebridge says the identity of the former officer should not be secret. (ABC News: Jerry Rickard)

The Greens spokesperson on Defence, David Shoebridge, said there was "no credible reason to hide the identity of the accused senior naval officer or the details of alleged offences".

"This is a court martial, overseen by very senior officers who are certainly capable of seeing past, and not being deflected by, media reporting of the trial," he said.

"Secrecy works for the interests of the government and Defence, but not for the public who deserve transparency and accountability.

"How are the public meant to have confidence in Defence's massive spending when Defence does not have confidence in public institutions and instead pushes corruption cases into closed military courts?"

World.title: Five of Sydney’s best homes that have stood the test of time
World.content:
PropertyNewsLuxury property Five of Sydney’s best homes that have stood the test of time Shona Hendley July 24, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There’s something special about an older home, one from a different era, with a sense of timelessness, character, history, good bones and quality workmanship. From Gothic, Georgian, Federation, Tudor, art deco and mid-century modern to Californian bungalows, here are five of the best homes in Sydney that have stood the test of time and are now for sale. 262 Johnston Street, Annandale, NSW This restored late-Victorian Gothic home is one of only three remaining “witches houses” in Annandale.



Known as “Highroyd”, the six-bedroom, four-level home, originally built in 1886 by renowned master builder John Young, is a National Trust Excellence Award winner, having taken out the 2009 Heritage Trust Commendation Award. Restored in the late 1980s by its current owners in collaboration with David Springett of Paragrid Architects, the conservation work included stonework, verandahs, gargoyles, stained glass and tessellated tiles. The home features a wine cellar, a library, an observation spire with city views, an indoor swimming pool and multiple living zones. 23 West Street, North Sydney



Located near St Leonards Park, this Victorian home in North Sydney was built about 1883. “The Colchester” features an iron lacework balcony and, inside, the home has been renovated by Rockpool Studios Design and rebuilt by JT Construct, with careful preservation of the original craftsmanship. The garden has been landscaped by The Palms Sydney. The property also features a wine cellar, skylights, a rooftop garden, a Monet Calacatta marble kitchen and a custom barbecue entertaining area. 196 Queen Street, Ashfield, NSW



This Californian bungalow sits on about 1206 square metres in Ashfield. The home welcomes you with its period façade while, inside, an open-plan living and dining area features soaring ceilings that capture the natural light and create a sense of spaciousness. There is an al fresco dining area at the rear, with landscaped gardens, a swimming pool and a garden pavilion. The home also features a secure garage, ducted air-conditioning and plantation shutters, and is within walking distance of Yeo Park and Ashfield Mall.



127 Pittwater Road, Manly, NSW This early-1900s cottage has been architecturally transformed to preserve its original character while accommodating contemporary living. Period features of the home include timber flooring, high ceilings, a tessellated-tile front porch, picture rails, ceiling roses, original brickwork and large bedrooms, one with an original fireplace. The contemporary kitchen features stone benchtops, engineered flooring and modern appliances.



Outside, there is a covered al fresco terrace with a fan, a gas cooktop and an electric blind. The home is close to Harris Farm Markets, eateries, schools and public transport. 158 Underwood Street, Paddington, NSW This three-level Victorian terrace is in one of Paddington’s most sought-after pockets, a quiet neighbourhood close to Oxford Street and within walking distance of the Sydney CBD.



It combines timeless period features, including ornate fireplaces and timber floorboards, with modern updates such as a contemporary kitchen with stone benchtops, a flexible layout and quality appliances and finishes. The property has a northerly frontage, 2½ bathrooms, three bedrooms, a rear courtyard and ample integrated storage. There is also a top-floor space that can be used as a retreat, office or bedroom.

World.title: NRL LIVE updates: Top-eight race hots up as Rabbitohs face Storm
World.content:
Sadly for South Sydney superstar Latrell Mitchell and Manly talisman Tom Trbojevic, cruel injuries have struck yet again in 2026, making their value on the open market a major talking point.

Should they both remain unsigned beyond November 1, you would ordinarily expect a bidding war for their services. But given how little football they have played in recent years, what is a fair price for them? At a time when the salary cap is about to increase, has their value gone up or down? Would it be possible to table a pay cut without offending the biggest names in the game?

These are the questions their clubs, as well as potential suitors, are asking themselves. When fit and firing, Mitchell and Trbojevic are the most dominant and captivating figures in the game.

In Mitchell’s case, there’s every chance he has played his last game of the year after consulting a neurologist about treatment for “complex nerve damage” relating to his back and calf issues. Trbojevic, meanwhile, is hopeful of a round 23 comeback against Melbourne after yet another hamstring strain. It’s his ninth in eight seasons.

The Sea Eagles had opened contract extension talks with Trbojevic’s management before his latest setback, while Souths have parked negotiations with Team Mitchell until their season ends. The Rabbitohs are hoping to retain the premiership-winning centre at a time when Campbell Graham, Brandon Smith, David Fifita, Tallis Duncan, Cody Walker and Jack Wighton are also about to become free agents.

NationalNSWNote From The Editor The mission to find Sydney’s best cafes Jordan Baker July 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

I love my morning coffee. On a cold July morning, the prospect of its warm, earthy goodness is one of the things that gets me out of bed. A good cuppa is a joy; a bad one can ruin a morning, less because of the taste than the disappointment. The ritual of buying a coffee can become part of the pleasure, particularly at a cafe with a sense of community. I still remember the jolt of delight I felt the first time a barista at the new-ish spot near the office remembered my order. The Herald’s eating out and restaurant editor Bianca Hrovat has visited more cafes than most, and for her, it’s this kind of warmth that makes a cafe stand out. Sydney has one of the best, and most interesting, cafe scenes in the world, thanks to places such as Solstice in Summer Hill. Dion Georgopoulos “My most memorable experiences when dining out at cafes or restaurants is when someone goes to the ends of the Earth to make you feel comfortable, and clearly wants to be there and is having a nice time,” she tells me. “I feel like it makes such a difference.” Sydney has one of the best, and most interesting, cafe scenes in the world. Amid so many excellent places, it can be hard to find the best; happily, the Good Food team has done the work for you, and is this week publishing its annual list of Sydney’s 100 Essential Cafes and Bakeries.



The guides include venues that are best for food, coffee, tea and matcha (I’ll never understand the matcha craze, but each to their own) as well as where to get the city’s best sweets, sandwiches, bread and baked goods, and institutions that continue to make our cities great. Sway in Manly serves up good vibes along with the coffee. Dion Georgopoulos We’ll have liftouts in our print publications today, Sunday, and on Friday and Sunday of next week. Our Good Food app will allow readers to search for cafes via an interactive map, browse custom collections, and filter down to the desired cuisine, dietary need, dining style or suburb. The app is available as a standalone subscription and is included in premium subscriptions to the Herald. Bianca began compiling this year’s guide almost immediately after finishing last year’s, and has been slowly eating and drinking her way across the city. The past few weeks have been a rush to visit new cafes; last Sunday she had four breakfasts, starting with one in Bondi at 7am and finishing at Guildford at 11. She is passionate about the important role cafes play in our lives, particularly during a cost-of-living crunch. “I don’t know if you’ve heard about the concept of little treat culture,” she says. “We don’t have much money to go out for dinner and things like that, but we still like to splurge on ourselves. So rather than spending $30 on a meal, we’ll spend a ridiculous amount of money on a croissant. It’s comparatively less, and it makes us feel good.”



It’s not just about the food and drink, though. As Bianca has reported, contemporary cafes are working hard to build a sense of community. Some host run clubs, or artisan markets, or coffee raves (a sober, daytime dance party). “The vibe is really important; they put a lot of effort into nurturing that,” says Bianca. “I think it’s almost as important as the food. They need each other.” Related Article Essential cafes and bakeries The 15 new cafes and bakeries drawing crowds, setting trends and remixing classics Bianca began her career as a news reporter in Queensland, and now combines her news background and food expertise for the Herald. She has won a Walkley award, alongside colleagues Eryk Bagshaw and Clare Sibthorpe, for her investigations into the sinister side of Sydney’s hospitality scene, and is nominated for a Logie for her work with Herald and 60 Minutes colleagues on a program about misconduct in the sector. While news reporting can be as challenging as it is rewarding, and isn’t for everyone, visiting cafes on the company dime sounds like a dream gig. “I really enjoy it,” she says. “I think the best part was getting to talk to people. Especially with cafes, the operators are usually independent, and they pour their hearts and souls into it.” The Good Food app is available as a standalone subscription and is included in premium digital Sydney Morning Herald subscriptions. Download it from the Apple App Store or the Google Play Store.

World.title: Queer venue’s closure signals religion’s enduring clout
World.content:
NationalCensorship Opinion Queer venue’s closure signals religion’s enduring clout Wendy Bacon Journalist and activist July 24, 2026 — 7:30pm

July 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

This month’s closure of Divine Playhouse in Sydney is the most recent episode in a long history of attacks on satirical artistic expression that offends certain conservative religious interests. Musicians and artists inside the now-defunct Divine Playhouse before it opened. Janie Barrett With no shortage of willing queer artists and followers, the Divine Playhouse promised to be a hilarious and inclusive pop-up venture. Artists dressed as nuns carrying sex toys and a mock communion were part of the spectacle. But the show had barely opened before it was shut down after about 100 right-wing Christians, including members of Prodigal Sons and Fit for the Kingdom, protested outside the venue. After building outrage on social media, the activists’ theatrical protest involved invoking saints and urging everyone to stand firm in the face of evil. The now-deserted building, which once served as a church but also as a poor house, homeless shelter and a community theatre, belongs to Revelop, which has an empire of residential, retail and commercial property developments.



The development company terminated Divine Playhouse’s one-year lease under breach of a clause which prohibited tenants from conducting “offensive trade” by mocking “sincerely held religious beliefs of millions of Christian Australians”. The clause originates from a mid-19th century law designed to combat foul smells from abattoirs. It was never intended to be an instrument of censorship. Related Article LGBTQ Sydney queer arts venue forced to close after Christian protests The eviction notice might survive a court challenge but in practice Divine Playhouse had to shut down and look for a new venue. The building is padlocked until the City of Sydney approves Revelop’s plan to demolish the surrounding buildings for luxury apartments, retail and a car park. The old building will become an upmarket bar, adding a heritage tone to the development. Revelop has arguably imposed an absolutist view of good and evil on a community, the vast majority of whom, including many practising Catholics, would not be agitated by the Playhouse.



This scenario takes me back to the late 1960s when we fought against notions of “moral depravity” which underpinned the old obscenity laws. Anti-censorship groups, tired of sitting through blacked-out sections of international movies, were picketing theatres. Publishing houses were too timid to produce challenging material by Australian authors. In 1970, I was one of the editors of UNSW student newspaper Tharunka when we determined to “act free by being free” and publish a supplement of censored literary works. For months, conservatives had called on the NSW government to crack down. A small group of right-wing evangelist students burnt Tharunkas, but thousands of others supported us. No action was taken until we published a poem, C--- is a Christian Word, which focused on repression in the Catholic Church. Priests delivered sermons demanding censorship. Finally, two of our team were summonsed to court. Defiant, we attended court dressed as nuns adorned with slogans from the poem. I was arrested wearing a habit with the words, “I have been f---ed by god’s steel prick.” Months later, a jury reached a compromise verdict that the poem was not obscene but the slogan on the nun’s costume was. A lawyer sent the poem to thousands of lawyers, informing them it was not obscene. This triggered more outrage from right-wing media, but the boundaries had shifted.



Wendy Bacon outside court after being convicted of setting, delivering or possessing an obscene or indecent publication; the November 1970 issue of Tharunka. John Patrick O'Gready/Fairfax Media By 1972, juries were declining to convict those charged with obscenities. A large number of summons were withdrawn or ended in minor penalties. The old censorship regime had fallen apart. By then gay liberation was on the rise. In 1981, gay liberationists donned nuns’ habits and formed a chapter of the Sisters of Perpetual Indulgence in Sydney. In the 1980s, three sisters were arrested for the slogan “anti-woman, anti-gay, fascist Pope go away!” during conservative Pope John Paul II’s visit. One street theatre involved exorcising the devil from Darlinghurst Police Station which was notorious for police violence and corruption. It is now the QTopia Sydney queer museum. By the 1990s, the Sisters were cheered by hundreds of thousands of annual Mardi Gras spectators. Today they conduct walking tours. While right-wing activists are spreading outrage about Create NSW granting $100,000 to Divine Playhouse, the Greens are pushing for the Minister for Music and Night-time Economy, John Graham, to support a further grant for the group to establish itself in a secure venue. A “Sing-in” protest is planned for Saturday in Hyde Park.



The queer community will survive this destructive blow and secure another venue. But this is far bigger than access to a venue and demonstrates why NSW badly needs a Human Rights Act. This is not an isolated incident. Conservative group Christian Lives Matter staged intimidating marches against the LGBTQ community in King Street Newtown in 2023 following The Project television program airing a sexual joke about Jesus earlier in the week. They, of course, do not represent Christian views generally. There is no denying the huge gains for the LGBTQ community over half a century. But today’s activists face different challenges. While we had the wind behind us, today’s activists need our support in standing their ground against headwinds from the far right, including conservative Christians in its ranks. Wendy Bacon is an independent journalist.

There’s something special about an older home, one from a different era, with a sense of timelessness, character, history, good bones and quality workmanship. From Gothic, Georgian, Art Deco, Federation, Tudor and mid-century modern to Californian bungalows, here are five of Melbourne’s best homes that have stood the test of time and are now for sale. 3 Wave Street, Elwood, VIC This double-storey period home in Elwood has been architecturally renovated to harmonise the property’s timeless character with contemporary, luxurious living.



Period features of the home include its facade, tiled front porch and window boxes, which offer a charming introduction. Related Article Auctions First home buyers battle for stylish $1.2m Northcote townhouse The rear of the home faces north, with soaring ceilings in the north-facing living, kitchen and dining areas filled with natural light. The kitchen includes a walk-in butler’s pantry, a self-cleaning oven, two dishwashers and a wine fridge. Oversized stackable glass sliding doors open to the backyard, which features a pool, outdoor shower, landscaped surrounds, lawn, gas-plumbed barbecue and an AstroTurf play area.



43 Bennett Street, Fitzroy North, VIC With a well-preserved, classic facade, this Victorian terrace is close to Edinburgh Gardens and Fitzroy North Village. The home’s interior combines period features, including high ceilings, stained-glass windows and fireplaces, with a modern rear extension featuring a dramatic raked ceiling and clerestory windows that capture northern light. There are two bedrooms, one with a corner fireplace and the second with built-in robes. There is also a central bathroom with classic checkerboard floor tiles, a bathtub and a heated towel rack.



62 St Phillip Street, Brunswick East, VIC Inner-north lifestyle meets period elegance. With four bedrooms, two bathrooms and a secure carport via rear lane access, this home in Brunswick East has lots to offer. Period features include decorative ceilings, oversized rooms, and a classic facade. Modern updates include a well-appointed kitchen with stone benchtops and stainless-steel appliances.



Large sliding doors open to a timber deck, a covered al fresco area and an established garden. There is also a separate outdoor laundry, bathroom and shed. 27 St Georges Road South, Fitzroy North, VIC This double-storey Victorian residence, built around 1876, evokes a sense of grandeur of a time gone by. The living room features soaring ceilings, a heritage ceiling rose and parquetry floors.



Related Article Auctions Brunswick East home discounted after auction to eventually sell for $1.69m There are four bedrooms, including one with built-in robes, and the apartment features access to a two-way bathroom. The central bathroom features full-height subway tiling, a mosaic-tiled floor and period-style tapware. Outside, there is a partially covered courtyard with a built-in barbecue, storage and roller-door access for parking. The home is in a corner position and is close to Edinburgh Gardens and Brunswick Street.



13 Hume Street, Armadale, VIC Set on a tree-lined street in Armadale, this freestanding Victorian home blends period features with modern living. Full-height steel-framed windows capture the northern light, while a marble-appointed kitchen with a vast island bench, bespoke cabinets and premium appliances offers modern luxury at its finest. Other features of the home include hydronic heating, air conditioning, a wine fridge, elegant timber floors, and a private north-facing courtyard with lush leafy borders, built-in seating and a barbecue area.

World.title: Uber blasts laws as it’s forced to reinstate banned driver
World.content:
Exclusive BusinessCompaniesUnfair dismissal Uber blasts laws as it’s forced to reinstate banned driver Elias Visontay July 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A workplace tribunal has ordered Uber to reinstate a driver it banned over 12 complaints alleging inappropriate touching, spitting on and swearing at passengers as well as speeding, as the rideshare giant continues to rally against the government’s gig economy worker protections. Uber’s loss follows a string of Fair Work Commission (FWC) decisions that have scolded the company’s complaints handling processes and repeatedly found it to have failed to properly engage with new laws introduced last year that give gig economy workers an employee-like appeals avenue to fight “deactivation” via the commission. Uber has lost another unfair deactivation appeal from a driver AP Despite the Albanese government last month amending the unfair deactivation code to help rideshare companies act quickly on sexual harassment allegations, Uber lost this case largely due to its failure to verify complaints and improperly informing the driver. While the deactivation at the centre of the case predates the amendment, Uber has said the outcome is proof that further changes are needed. A consistent theme in its FWC losses is its reliance on unverified customer complaints without providing further evidence, which Uber claims is to avoid re-traumatising riders.



In the latest case, Uber deactivated a Melbourne driver who worked on the platform from December 2021 until November 2025, over 12 rider complaints. Related Article Exclusive

Harassment How banned Uber drivers are reinstated, while passenger evidence goes unheard The historic complaints alleged aggressive language, dangerous driving, disputes over luggage, and physical altercations including pushing a rider. In multiple instances, Uber suspended the driver but later reinstated him after he denied the claims. This included a 2025 incident involving alleged inappropriate touching where GPS data contradicted the rider’s complaint. Another incident that led to a temporary suspension and subsequent reactivation included a claim that the driver pushed a passenger and forced them out of his car after picking them up on Chapel Street. The driver denied wrongdoing, telling an Uber investigator the passengers he picked up were drunk, and pulled his handbrake while in motion, so he asked them to leave his vehicle.



Others claimed he kicked them out of his car for smelling of cigarettes; threatened to hurt them and asked for extra money for having had to wait for them; was speeding and using his phone; told a solo female rider to “f--- off” after getting angry for having to wait for her; and tried to stop a group taking their luggage out of his car after they closed their door with the seatbelt slung outside which scratched the frame. His final complaint in November 2025 alleged he became “extremely hostile”, used profanity, and spat at a group of customers with a pet. The rider suspected the outburst was racially motivated. “As a Chinese person, I suspect that he may have acted this way because he saw that we are Asian,” the complaint continued. Uber immediately suspended the driver, but the rider did not respond to follow-up requests for more information. Despite the driver denying the claims, Uber permanently terminated his account shortly after, prompting his FWC appeal. “He said that he was a family oriented, religious and respectful individual and the complaints were entirely baseless,” Commissioner Oanh Thi Tran said. At the FWC, the driver argued Uber had not followed the fair process and given him the opportunity to respond to complaints.



Uber, meanwhile, argued the deactivation was valid to preserve rider safety, claiming the sheer volume of complaints meant they were likely true. Related Article Exclusive

Disability Uber stands by sacking of driver who refused guide dog It also argued it was exempt from needing to issue formal warnings – as required under the law – because the pattern of behaviour made it unsafe for him to keep working. However, Tran found the deactivation unlawful. Crucially, Uber directly asked the driver to respond to only three of the 12 complaints over his four-year tenure. Four complaints were never put to him. Tran found the deactivation was unfair, and that Uber had not proved why it had deemed the driver’s behaviour so concerning that it was entitled to the exemption to suspend him without issuing a formal warning.



Without the exemption, this meant Uber needed to follow the process of informing the driver of complaints and giving him a chance to respond, which Tran found it failed to do. Tran found Uber breached the code by not giving the driver a fair chance to respond. She also ruled Uber failed to prove the alleged conduct actually occurred, noting its reliance on “hearsay”. “Uber have accepted the veracity of the entirety of the rider’s complaints without having regard to [the driver’s] denial of it,” Tran said in relation to the final complaint that led to the termination. Tran ordered Uber to reactivate the driver and pay lost wages based on his $1118 weekly average. He claimed Uber was his main source of income with which he supported his family of three children. Nicole Ashcroft, Head of Safety for Uber, said “this case is a clear example of the continued limitations of the current system”. “This case involved 12 complaints covering interpersonal conflict and dangerous driving, backed up by rider complaints and platform data,” she said.



“The code changes fail to address evidence issues and we are concerned the Fair Work Commission continues to fail to recognise the nature of platform work by not giving proper weight to patterns of complaint,” Ashcroft said, adding that “urgent reform” was needed. Responding to Uber’s complaints, a spokesperson for workplace minister Amanda Rishworth said “the amendments were developed in consultation with stakeholders, including digital platforms and unions”. World.title: Chad Warner reveals why he keeps investing in the Sydney Swans
World.content:
SportAFLSydney Swans Chad Warner reveals why he keeps investing in the Sydney Swans Jonathan Drennan July 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Seven years ago, Perth-raised Chad Warner nervously waited to get drafted into the AFL. He knew it was down to two clubs: the Sydney Swans and the GWS Giants. “It was pretty cool to be of interest to either team, but I’m very happy that the Swans jumped in and I think I’m at the right place,” he said. Sydney Swan Chad Warner has found a new side to the city he has called home for seven years. Rhett Wyman “The day before the draft, my manager said that he thought the two frontrunners were both Sydney teams. “I literally just wanted a contract wherever it was. It was probably a bit of a surprise hearing the two Sydney teams were interested.”



Two years ago, Warner signed a contract extension to keep him at the Swans until the end of 2027. The 25-year-old has been open about the pull of returning to Perth, but has built strong roots in the harbour city and is a key part of the Swans’ push towards a flag, which continues against GWS in Saturday’s 33rd Sydney derby. The Swans are second on the ladder, but have lost three of their past four games. Warner has been a bright spot in Sydney’s recent lull, moving principally to the midfield after round 12, having spent time in the forward pocket earlier in the season. The move has helped him unlock some strong individual form for a Swans’ team desperate for a win. Chad Warner has been a bright spot for a disappointing Swans team recently. Getty Images “I feel like, probably over the last couple of months, I’ve been playing some pretty solid, consistent footy,” Warner said. “I’ve been focusing more on trying to get first possession from clearances, centre bounces and stoppage clearances. I think I’ve been able to contribute a bit more there, which is great.



“Tackling and contested footy are things you can control a bit more than kicking goals, so it’s more of a focus point to come back to. “I chatted with the coaches about me playing more stoppages and more midfield time to help Isaac [Heeney] out a bit, because he was probably doing the brunt of the clearance work – it’s about giving him a bit of a chop out [break] if he’s getting tired.” Isaac Heeney is expected to play against the Giants on Saturday despite nursing a sore back. Getty Images Heeney will need all the help he can get after nursing a sore back against Adelaide, but is expected to play against the Giants. Warner is also aware of the dangers the inconsistent GWS pose on Saturday at Sydney Olympic Park, despite their recent shock loss to Essendon. “For the top-of-the-table clashes and the big games, they [the Giants] really get themselves up for them,” Warner said. “They’ve beaten Brisbane, Hawthorn and Fremantle, so they’ve beaten all the top teams, which shows their calibre and capability.”



Off the field, Warner finally feels at home in Sydney after initially struggling to adjust to life outside Perth. Succeeding in football has always come naturally, but a new home in Paddington and working in investment management one day a week have helped Warner feel more at home. The midfielder doesn’t believe the pre-draft teenage Warner would believe what has happened to him. “At the age of 18, I genuinely would have thought it was a totally different person [looking at himself now], I would have thought he was absolutely joking,” he said. “I couldn’t care less about investing then, I was much more of a hands-on, labourer-type worker.



“Living in Paddington is probably something I never thought I’d do either. I thought I’d be on a [rural] property somewhere ... “When you’re an 18-year-old over in Perth wanting to get drafted and play AFL, all you’re thinking about is kicking the ball and playing AFL.” Cox and Swans ready for ‘spiteful’ Sydney derby Sydney Swans coach Dean Cox believes that despite the gap between his side and the Giants on the AFL ladder, the teams will deliver a typically “spiteful” game of football in Saturday’s derby. The Swans are second on the ladder despite two losses in three games, while the Giants are just outside a finals spot in 11th after losing to Essendon in Melbourne on Sunday.



Cox is aware of the Giants’ ability to spring surprises this season, including victories over premiership contenders Fremantle, Brisbane, Geelong and Hawthorn. “I think they [Sydney derbies] are always quite intense; I think no matter where the sides are on the ladder, or the form that they do come in with, this is a very spiteful, intense game of football,” Cox said. Sydney derbies have been known to get physical in the past. Channel Seven “It’s always great to take on the crosstown rivals. One thing we’re preparing our group for is what they’ve done against the best football teams, and that’s where our mind space needs to be.” Cox has demanded a stronger four-quarter effort from his team, after falling away late in the game in losses to Adelaide and Fremantle.



“For periods, we’ve been really good in it [the fourth quarter],” he said. “The whole part about it is consistency and how often can we do it. “When the times come, we’ve certainly had last quarters or periods in games against the best teams where we’ve actually stood out in that area. It’s just about trying to make sure that we can do it as well as we can for as long as we can.” Cox also said he wants the team to be collectively responsible for reacting when momentum changes during games. “Whether it’s the leadership group, the emerging leaders that we have, everyone that’s out on the field at that particular time has to take the moment when it’s there,” Cox said. “We’ve let ourselves down at times in that period, but as I mentioned before, we’ve also had some players that have really risen to the occasion and got our team over the line.”



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Should not have happened’: Dillon, Crows denounce booing after coach comes under fire Billy Cootee gets a rare opportunity for the Swans, having played just four games this season, after consistently impressing in the VFL. Cox believes that Cootee’s work rate and ability to kick goals are needed against a Giants team whose season is hanging in the balance. “With Billy, he’s been in form for over a month,” Cox said. “The thing I like about what Billy’s been able to do is that he’s gone back after experiencing AFL footy. “He’s learnt from what the difference is between SANFL as well as VFL and now AFL. I think certainly on the weekend, it’s not only his ability to finish off in front of goal but his work rate and his 13 tackles, his pressure he puts on the opposition was enormous. We need to make sure that we give him every opportunity to play well.”

World.title: Five of Sydney’s best homes that have stood the test of time
World.content:
PropertyNewsLuxury property Five of Sydney’s best homes that have stood the test of time Shona Hendley July 24, 2026 — 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There’s something special about an older home, one from a different era, with a sense of timelessness, character, history, good bones and quality workmanship. From Gothic, Georgian, Federation, Tudor, art deco and mid-century modern to Californian bungalows, here are five of the best homes in Sydney that have stood the test of time and are now for sale. 262 Johnston Street, Annandale, NSW This restored late-Victorian Gothic home is one of only three remaining “witches houses” in Annandale.



Known as “Highroyd”, the six-bedroom, four-level home, originally built in 1886 by renowned master builder John Young, is a National Trust Excellence Award winner, having taken out the 2009 Heritage Trust Commendation Award. Restored in the late 1980s by its current owners in collaboration with David Springett of Paragrid Architects, the conservation work included stonework, verandahs, gargoyles, stained glass and tessellated tiles. The home features a wine cellar, a library, an observation spire with city views, an indoor swimming pool and multiple living zones. 23 West Street, North Sydney



Located near St Leonards Park, this Victorian home in North Sydney was built about 1883. “The Colchester” features an iron lacework balcony and, inside, the home has been renovated by Rockpool Studios Design and rebuilt by JT Construct, with careful preservation of the original craftsmanship. The garden has been landscaped by The Palms Sydney. The property also features a wine cellar, skylights, a rooftop garden, a Monet Calacatta marble kitchen and a custom barbecue entertaining area. 196 Queen Street, Ashfield, NSW



This Californian bungalow sits on about 1206 square metres in Ashfield. The home welcomes you with its period façade while, inside, an open-plan living and dining area features soaring ceilings that capture the natural light and create a sense of spaciousness. There is an al fresco dining area at the rear, with landscaped gardens, a swimming pool and a garden pavilion. The home also features a secure garage, ducted air-conditioning and plantation shutters, and is within walking distance of Yeo Park and Ashfield Mall.



127 Pittwater Road, Manly, NSW This early-1900s cottage has been architecturally transformed to preserve its original character while accommodating contemporary living. Period features of the home include timber flooring, high ceilings, a tessellated-tile front porch, picture rails, ceiling roses, original brickwork and large bedrooms, one with an original fireplace. The contemporary kitchen features stone benchtops, engineered flooring and modern appliances.



Outside, there is a covered al fresco terrace with a fan, a gas cooktop and an electric blind. The home is close to Harris Farm Markets, eateries, schools and public transport. 158 Underwood Street, Paddington, NSW This three-level Victorian terrace is in one of Paddington’s most sought-after pockets, a quiet neighbourhood close to Oxford Street and within walking distance of the Sydney CBD.



It combines timeless period features, including ornate fireplaces and timber floorboards, with modern updates such as a contemporary kitchen with stone benchtops, a flexible layout and quality appliances and finishes. The property has a northerly frontage, 2½ bathrooms, three bedrooms, a rear courtyard and ample integrated storage. There is also a top-floor space that can be used as a retreat, office or bedroom.

World.title: NRL LIVE updates: Top-eight race hots up as Rabbitohs face Storm
World.content:
Sadly for South Sydney superstar Latrell Mitchell and Manly talisman Tom Trbojevic, cruel injuries have struck yet again in 2026, making their value on the open market a major talking point.

Should they both remain unsigned beyond November 1, you would ordinarily expect a bidding war for their services. But given how little football they have played in recent years, what is a fair price for them? At a time when the salary cap is about to increase, has their value gone up or down? Would it be possible to table a pay cut without offending the biggest names in the game?

These are the questions their clubs, as well as potential suitors, are asking themselves. When fit and firing, Mitchell and Trbojevic are the most dominant and captivating figures in the game.

In Mitchell’s case, there’s every chance he has played his last game of the year after consulting a neurologist about treatment for “complex nerve damage” relating to his back and calf issues. Trbojevic, meanwhile, is hopeful of a round 23 comeback against Melbourne after yet another hamstring strain. It’s his ninth in eight seasons.

The Sea Eagles had opened contract extension talks with Trbojevic’s management before his latest setback, while Souths have parked negotiations with Team Mitchell until their season ends. The Rabbitohs are hoping to retain the premiership-winning centre at a time when Campbell Graham, Brandon Smith, David Fifita, Tallis Duncan, Cody Walker and Jack Wighton are also about to become free agents.

The now-deserted building, which once served as a church but also as a poor house, homeless shelter and a community theatre, belongs to Revelop, which has an empire of residential, retail and commercial property developments.



The development company terminated Divine Playhouse’s one-year lease under breach of a clause which prohibited tenants from conducting “offensive trade” by mocking “sincerely held religious beliefs of millions of Christian Australians”. The clause originates from a mid-19th century law designed to combat foul smells from abattoirs. It was never intended to be an instrument of censorship. Related Article LGBTQ Sydney queer arts venue forced to close after Christian protests The eviction notice might survive a court challenge but in practice Divine Playhouse had to shut down and look for a new venue. The building is padlocked until the City of Sydney approves Revelop’s plan to demolish the surrounding buildings for luxury apartments, retail and a car park. The old building will become an upmarket bar, adding a heritage tone to the development. Revelop has arguably imposed an absolutist view of good and evil on a community, the vast majority of whom, including many practising Catholics, would not be agitated by the Playhouse.



This scenario takes me back to the late 1960s when we fought against notions of “moral depravity” which underpinned the old obscenity laws. Anti-censorship groups, tired of sitting through blacked-out sections of international movies, were picketing theatres. Publishing houses were too timid to produce challenging material by Australian authors. In 1970, I was one of the editors of UNSW student newspaper Tharunka when we determined to “act free by being free” and publish a supplement of censored literary works. For months, conservatives had called on the NSW government to crack down. A small group of right-wing evangelist students burnt Tharunkas, but thousands of others supported us. No action was taken until we published a poem, C--- is a Christian Word, which focused on repression in the Catholic Church. Priests delivered sermons demanding censorship. Finally, two of our team were summonsed to court. Defiant, we attended court dressed as nuns adorned with slogans from the poem. I was arrested wearing a habit with the words, “I have been f---ed by god’s steel prick.” Months later, a jury reached a compromise verdict that the poem was not obscene but the slogan on the nun’s costume was. A lawyer sent the poem to thousands of lawyers, informing them it was not obscene. This triggered more outrage from right-wing media, but the boundaries had shifted.



Wendy Bacon outside court after being convicted of setting, delivering or possessing an obscene or indecent publication; the November 1970 issue of Tharunka. John Patrick O'Gready/Fairfax Media By 1972, juries were declining to convict those charged with obscenities. A large number of summons were withdrawn or ended in minor penalties. The old censorship regime had fallen apart. By then gay liberation was on the rise. In 1981, gay liberationists donned nuns’ habits and formed a chapter of the Sisters of Perpetual Indulgence in Sydney. In the 1980s, three sisters were arrested for the slogan “anti-woman, anti-gay, fascist Pope go away!” during conservative Pope John Paul II’s visit. One street theatre involved exorcising the devil from Darlinghurst Police Station which was notorious for police violence and corruption. It is now the QTopia Sydney queer museum. By the 1990s, the Sisters were cheered by hundreds of thousands of annual Mardi Gras spectators. Today they conduct walking tours. While right-wing activists are spreading outrage about Create NSW granting $100,000 to Divine Playhouse, the Greens are pushing for the Minister for Music and Night-time Economy, John Graham, to support a further grant for the group to establish itself in a secure venue. A “Sing-in” protest is planned for Saturday in Hyde Park.



The queer community will survive this destructive blow and secure another venue. But this is far bigger than access to a venue and demonstrates why NSW badly needs a Human Rights Act. This is not an isolated incident. Conservative group Christian Lives Matter staged intimidating marches against the LGBTQ community in King Street Newtown in 2023 following The Project television program airing a sexual joke about Jesus earlier in the week. They, of course, do not represent Christian views generally. There is no denying the huge gains for the LGBTQ community over half a century. But today’s activists face different challenges. While we had the wind behind us, today’s activists need our support in standing their ground against headwinds from the far right, including conservative Christians in its ranks. Wendy Bacon is an independent journalist.

There’s something special about an older home, one from a different era, with a sense of timelessness, character, history, good bones and quality workmanship. Period features of the home include its facade, tiled front porch and window boxes, which offer a charming introduction. Related Article Auctions First home buyers battle for stylish $1.2m Northcote townhouse The rear of the home faces north, with soaring ceilings in the north-facing living, kitchen and dining areas filled with natural light. Oversized stackable glass sliding doors open to the backyard, which features a pool, outdoor shower, landscaped surrounds, lawn, gas-plumbed barbecue and an AstroTurf play area.



43 Bennett Street, Fitzroy North, VIC With a well-preserved, classic facade, this Victorian terrace is close to Edinburgh Gardens and Fitzroy North Village. The home’s interior combines period features, including high ceilings, stained-glass windows and fireplaces, with a modern rear extension featuring a dramatic raked ceiling and clerestory windows that capture northern light. There are two bedrooms, one with a corner fireplace and the second with built-in robes. There is also a central bathroom with classic checkerboard floor tiles, a bathtub and a heated towel rack.



62 St Phillip Street, Brunswick East, VIC Inner-north lifestyle meets period elegance. With four bedrooms, two bathrooms and a secure carport via rear lane access, this home in Brunswick East has lots to offer. Period features include decorative ceilings, oversized rooms, and a classic facade. Modern updates include a well-appointed kitchen with stone benchtops and stainless-steel appliances.



Large sliding doors open to a timber deck, a covered al fresco area and an established garden. Related Article Auctions Brunswick East home discounted after auction to eventually sell for $1.69m There are four bedrooms, including one with built-in robes, and the apartment features access to a two-way bathroom. 13 Hume Street, Armadale, VIC Set on a tree-lined street in Armadale, this freestanding Victorian home blends period features with modern living. Full-height steel-framed windows capture the northern light, while a marble-appointed kitchen with a vast island bench, bespoke cabinets and premium appliances offers modern luxury at its finest. World.title: Uber blasts laws as it’s forced to reinstate banned driver
World.content:
Exclusive BusinessCompaniesUnfair dismissal Uber blasts laws as it’s forced to reinstate banned driver Elias Visontay July 24, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A workplace tribunal has ordered Uber to reinstate a driver it banned over 12 complaints alleging inappropriate touching, spitting on and swearing at passengers as well as speeding, as the rideshare giant continues to rally against the government’s gig economy worker protections. Uber’s loss follows a string of Fair Work Commission (FWC) decisions that have scolded the company’s complaints handling processes and repeatedly found it to have failed to properly engage with new laws introduced last year that give gig economy workers an employee-like appeals avenue to fight “deactivation” via the commission. Uber has lost another unfair deactivation appeal from a driver AP Despite the Albanese government last month amending the unfair deactivation code to help rideshare companies act quickly on sexual harassment allegations, Uber lost this case largely due to its failure to verify complaints and improperly informing the driver. While the deactivation at the centre of the case predates the amendment, Uber has said the outcome is proof that further changes are needed. A consistent theme in its FWC losses is its reliance on unverified customer complaints without providing further evidence, which Uber claims is to avoid re-traumatising riders.



In the latest case, Uber deactivated a Melbourne driver who worked on the platform from December 2021 until November 2025, over 12 rider complaints. Related Article Exclusive

Harassment How banned Uber drivers are reinstated, while passenger evidence goes unheard The historic complaints alleged aggressive language, dangerous driving, disputes over luggage, and physical altercations including pushing a rider. In multiple instances, Uber suspended the driver but later reinstated him after he denied the claims. This included a 2025 incident involving alleged inappropriate touching where GPS data contradicted the rider’s complaint. Another incident that led to a temporary suspension and subsequent reactivation included a claim that the driver pushed a passenger and forced them out of his car after picking them up on Chapel Street. The driver denied wrongdoing, telling an Uber investigator the passengers he picked up were drunk, and pulled his handbrake while in motion, so he asked them to leave his vehicle.



Others claimed he kicked them out of his car for smelling of cigarettes; threatened to hurt them and asked for extra money for having had to wait for them; was speeding and using his phone; told a solo female rider to “f--- off” after getting angry for having to wait for her; and tried to stop a group taking their luggage out of his car after they closed their door with the seatbelt slung outside which scratched the frame. His final complaint in November 2025 alleged he became “extremely hostile”, used profanity, and spat at a group of customers with a pet. The rider suspected the outburst was racially motivated. “As a Chinese person, I suspect that he may have acted this way because he saw that we are Asian,” the complaint continued. Uber immediately suspended the driver, but the rider did not respond to follow-up requests for more information. Despite the driver denying the claims, Uber permanently terminated his account shortly after, prompting his FWC appeal. “He said that he was a family oriented, religious and respectful individual and the complaints were entirely baseless,” Commissioner Oanh Thi Tran said. At the FWC, the driver argued Uber had not followed the fair process and given him the opportunity to respond to complaints.



Uber, meanwhile, argued the deactivation was valid to preserve rider safety, claiming the sheer volume of complaints meant they were likely true. Related Article Exclusive

Disability Uber stands by sacking of driver who refused guide dog It also argued it was exempt from needing to issue formal warnings – as required under the law – because the pattern of behaviour made it unsafe for him to keep working. However, Tran found the deactivation unlawful. Crucially, Uber directly asked the driver to respond to only three of the 12 complaints over his four-year tenure. Four complaints were never put to him. Tran found the deactivation was unfair, and that Uber had not proved why it had deemed the driver’s behaviour so concerning that it was entitled to the exemption to suspend him without issuing a formal warning.



Without the exemption, this meant Uber needed to follow the process of informing the driver of complaints and giving him a chance to respond, which Tran found it failed to do. Tran found Uber breached the code by not giving the driver a fair chance to respond. She also ruled Uber failed to prove the alleged conduct actually occurred, noting its reliance on “hearsay”. “Uber have accepted the veracity of the entirety of the rider’s complaints without having regard to [the driver’s] denial of it,” Tran said in relation to the final complaint that led to the termination. Tran ordered Uber to reactivate the driver and pay lost wages based on his $1118 weekly average. He claimed Uber was his main source of income with which he supported his family of three children. Nicole Ashcroft, Head of Safety for Uber, said “this case is a clear example of the continued limitations of the current system”. “This case involved 12 complaints covering interpersonal conflict and dangerous driving, backed up by rider complaints and platform data,” she said.



“The code changes fail to address evidence issues and we are concerned the Fair Work Commission continues to fail to recognise the nature of platform work by not giving proper weight to patterns of complaint,” Ashcroft said, adding that “urgent reform” was needed. Responding to Uber’s complaints, a spokesperson for workplace minister Amanda Rishworth said “the amendments were developed in consultation with stakeholders, including digital platforms and unions”.
